 1          The Personal Injury and School District Plaintiffs (“PISD Plaintiffs”) and Defendants Meta

 2   Platforms, Inc. and Instagram LLC (together, “Meta”) (collectively, the “Parties”) submit this Joint Report

 3   and jointly move the Court to select and appoint a special master under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 53

 4   to oversee Meta’s re-review of documents withheld or redacted for privilege or work product.

 5          WHEREAS, by email to the Court dated October 10, 2026, Meta agreed to submit to independent

 6   special master oversight of a re-review of the documents it withheld in full or redacted for privilege or work

 7   product;

 8          WHEREAS, the Parties have agreed to submit the special master candidates identified in Section I

 9   below for the Court’s consideration and to ask the Court to select and appoint one of them as special master

10   (the “Special Master”);

11          WHEREAS, Meta has agreed to pay the Special Master’s fees and costs;

12          WHEREAS, Rule 53(a)(1)(A) authorizes the Court to appoint a master to perform duties to which

13   the parties consent, and Rule 53(b)(1) permits any party to suggest candidates for appointment; and

14          WHEREAS, the Parties continue to meet and confer on a protocol to govern the re-review and the

15   Special Master’s duties, and will submit an agreed protocol, or competing proposals on any disputed terms,

16   by close of business Monday, October 19, 2026;

17          NOW, THEREFORE, the Parties report and jointly move as follows:

18   I.     PROPOSED CANDIDATES
19          The Parties submit the following candidates for the Court’s consideration. Each candidate’s résumé

20   is attached as an exhibit. Each candidate has confirmed availability to begin promptly and has identified no

21   conflict with any Party.

22          A.      Plaintiffs’ Proposed Candidates
23          Hon. Lawrence F. Stengel (Ret.). Judge Stengel served as the court-appointed special master

24   handling deposition designation disputes in the Tennessee Attorney General’s case against Meta, which

25   gives him direct and significant experience with the issues in this case that would permit him to readily

26   grasp the nature and context of the materials he would review here. A former Chief Judge of the Eastern

27   District of Pennsylvania, he also serves as Special Discovery Master in the Generic Pharmaceuticals Pricing

28   MDL. (Résumé attached as Ex. A; $1,200 per hour, $500 per hour for associates.)
                                                      -1-
          JOINT REPORT AND MOTION TO SELECT AND APPOINT A SPECIAL MASTER TO OVERSEE META PRIVILEGE RE-REVIEW
                                                   4:22-md-03047-YGR
               Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR            Document 3571         Filed 10/15/26      Page 3 of 7



 1          Daniel B. Garrie. As Special Master appointed by Judge Chhabria in In re Facebook, Inc.

 2   Consumer Privacy User Profile Litigation, 655 F. Supp. 3d 899, 907, 913 (N.D. Cal. 2023), Mr. Garrie

 3   reviewed thousands of documents Meta (then Facebook) claimed as privileged and adjudicated other

 4   discovery disputes, and his determinations were upheld when challenged. That work gives him direct

 5   experience applying Ninth Circuit privilege law to Meta’s documents, along with firsthand knowledge of its

 6   privilege practices during an overlapping period, allowing him to assess Meta’s claims here quickly and

 7   cost-effectively. (Résumé attached as Ex. B; $900 per hour, $500 per hour for other lawyers.)

 8          David R. Cohen. Federal courts have appointed Mr. Cohen special master in more than 30 complex

 9   cases, including a District of Kansas appointment on attorney-client privilege issues and a role as Special

10   Master in In re National Prescription Opiate Litigation, MDL No. 2804 (N.D. Ohio), where his duties also

11   include ruling on privilege issues. He edited and co-authored Appointing Special Masters and Other

12   Judicial Adjuncts, a benchbook for federal judges, giving him command of the procedures that make a

13   court-supervised privilege re-review fair, efficient, and durable on review. (Résumé attached as Ex. C; $900

14   per hour blended rate.)

15          Plaintiffs do not question the qualifications of Meta’s proposed candidates. But Plaintiffs’ candidates

16   have more direct and substantial experience with the issues presented here, which will enable them to

17   perform this role more efficiently and reliably. Plaintiffs’ candidates also warrant additional weight because

18   Meta’s improper privilege process made this re-review necessary.

19          B.      Meta’s Proposed Candidates
20          Meta respectfully submits that the appropriate profile for the special master is a former Magistrate

21   Judge who was deeply involved in Ninth Circuit and California law involving attorney-client privilege and

22   work product protections, given that these issues lie at the heart of the re-review process. For that reason,

23   Meta proposes the selection of either Hon. Suzanne Segal (ret.) or Hon. Karen Crawford (ret.) (bios

24   attached as Exs. D and E), both of whom had long tenures as Magistrate Judges in California and whose

25   case managers confirmed their availability to serve as special masters overseeing this review process at rates

26   Meta will pay in full ($1500-$1700/hour, or $15,000-$17,000/day).

27          Judge Segal served as a Magistrate Judge for 18 years in the Central District of California, including

28   four years as the Chief Magistrate Judge, was previously appointed by the Court to serve as a special master
                                                         -2-
          JOINT REPORT AND MOTION TO SELECT AND APPOINT A SPECIAL MASTER TO OVERSEE META PRIVILEGE RE-REVIEW
                                                   4:22-md-03047-YGR
               Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR             Document 3571         Filed 10/15/26      Page 4 of 7



 1   in the Epic v. Apple privilege re-review, and also served as a special master in United States v. United

 2   Health Group, No. CV-16-8697, C.D. Cal (FMO) (SSx), which likewise involved substantial privilege

 3   issues under Ninth Circuit law.

 4          Judge Crawford served as a Magistrate Judge in the Southern District of California for 14 years,

 5   until earlier this year, including serving as the Presiding Magistrate Judge from 2024-25, and as a Magistrate

 6   Judge issued numerous decisions on attorney-client privilege and work product protections under Ninth

 7   Circuit law and (like Judge Segal) would be ideally suited to preside over the privilege re-review.

 8          By contrast, none of Plaintiffs’ three candidates (all of whom are based on the East Coast) has any

 9   particular background or expertise in applying the standards of attorney-client privilege and work product

10   protection under Ninth Circuit law, and neither Mr. Garrie nor Mr. Cohen has ever served as a judge. Both

11   Mr. Garrie and Mr. Cohen have close ties to the MDL Plaintiffs’ bar (as reflected in the fact that Plaintiffs’

12   counsel contacted them directly, rather than through case administrators), Mr. Garrie has never been a

13   practicing lawyer, and Mr. Cohen has two years of law practice experience. All three of Plaintiffs’

14   candidates are carrying significant ongoing roles in other matters and have furnished associate (or blended)

15   billing rates to Plaintiffs’ counsel, reflecting that they will oversee the work of unnamed associates at their

16   respective firms as opposed to doing their own work (as both Judge Segal and Judge Crawford intend to do).

17   II.    RELIEF REQUESTED
18          The Parties respectfully request that the Court:

19          1.      Select one of the candidates identified in Section I and appoint that candidate as Special

20   Master under Rule 53(a)(1)(A) to oversee Meta’s privilege re-review;

21          2.      Direct the selected candidate to file the affidavit required by Rule 53(b)(3)(A), disclosing

22   whether any ground exists for disqualification under 28 U.S.C. § 455;

23          3.      Order Meta to pay the Special Master’s fees and costs; and

24          4.      Direct the Parties to submit, by close of business Monday, October 19, 2026, an agreed re-

25   review protocol, or competing proposals on any disputed terms, together with a proposed order of

26   appointment that complies with Rule 53(b)(2).

27          A proposed order accompanies this motion.

Experience
Hon. Lawrence F. Stengel (Ret.) is the Chief Executive Officer of Optimal Dispute Resolutions. He works with parties or counsel
to mediate or arbitrate disputes in all areas of the law, with a focus on the fair resolution of each case in a professional, ethical,
and practical manner. His 28-year judicial career has prepared him to take an objective, realistic, and credible approach to the
mediation/arbitration process and provide effective resolutions in complex, multi-party matters.

Judge Stengel brings a wealth of experience to Optimal, having tried patent and trade secret cases, complex product liability
cases, MDLs, premises liability, employment discrimination, complex civil and criminal fraud, complicated custody cases, family
business disputes, and hundreds of criminal cases.

Prior to leading Optimal Dispute Resolutions, Judge Stengel served as the Chief Judge of the United States District Court for the
Eastern District of Pennsylvania. Judge Stengel has proudly served the community for nearly three decades, serving for 14 years
as a United States District Judge for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania (EDPA) and 14 years on the Lancaster County Court of
Common Pleas.

From 1990 until 2004, Stengel served as a judge on the Lancaster County Court of Common Pleas where he presided over
hundreds of trials, jury and nonjury; wrote hundreds of opinions; and conducted settlement conferences in numerous cases.
He handled 20 homicide cases, two of which were capital cases that went to trial. His state court work included many complex
negligence, product liability, professional malpractice, land use, and commercial cases involving trials, hearings, motions, and
settlements. In 2003, he was nominated to a seat on the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania by
President George W. Bush. He was confirmed by the United States Senate on June 16, 2004.

Early in his career, from 1980 to 1984, he was in private practice in Pittsburgh with Dickie, McCarney, and Chilcote, P.C. He then
began his own practice in Lancaster with his father, Lawrence E. Stengel, from 1985 until 1990.

At the federal level, Judge Stengel has written hundreds of opinions and has presided over dozens of civil and criminal trials,
including two Multi-District Litigation cases. In 2009 he was appointed to the Judicial Conference Committee on Judicial
Resources, the committee responsible for human resources policy for the entire federal judiciary. He was subsequently named
Chairman of the Committee by Chief Justice Roberts in 2015.

Judge Stengel received a Bachelor of Arts from Saint Joseph’s University in 1974 and a Juris Doctor from the University of
Pittsburgh School of Law in 1980. While in law school, he served on the Law Review and published a Comment. He was a teacher
at Lancaster Catholic High School from 1974 until 1977; an adjunct professor at Millersville University from 2000 to 2004; an
adjunct professor at Franklin and Marshall College for 21 years, from 1997 to 2018; and an adjunct professor at the Beasley
School of Law at Temple University from 2013 to 2018.

                                 DANIEL B. GARRIE, ESQ.
          Orlando, Florida 32827 | O: (855) 529-2466 | E: daniel@lawandforensics.com

Daniel Garrie is the founder of Law & Forensics LLC and the head of the Computer Forensics
Practice Group. A licensed attorney with bachelor’s and master’s degrees in computer science and
more than 20 years of technical and legal experience, Mr. Garrie is a nationally recognized expert
in cybersecurity, digital forensics, data privacy, ediscovery, digital evidence, and complex
technology systems.

Mr. Garrie has served as a special master, discovery referee, forensic neutral, arbitrator, and
mediator in state and federal courts, administrative proceedings, and arbitrations. Since joining
JAMS in 2016, he has presided over complex disputes involving large-scale electronically stored
information, digital forensic evidence, data privacy, cybersecurity controls, and cloud and
enterprise technology environments. Judge Chhabria appointed him eDiscovery Special Master in
In re: Facebook, Inc. Consumer Privacy User Profile Litigation. In that role, he issued dozens of
orders resolving disputes over the production of data from one of the world’s largest data
processors and monitored dozens of technical depositions. He has also served as eDiscovery
Special Master in federal class actions and as Special Master in a large-scale, multi-party oil spill
case. He has been a Discovery Referee in dozens of Los Angeles Superior Court disputes and in
numerous other states. He is an eDiscovery Special Master for the U.S. District Court, Western
District of Pennsylvania, and was named a Distinguished Neutral by the Academy of Court
Appointed Masters in 2015.

As a consulting and testifying expert, Mr. Garrie has advised clients and courts on data breaches,
cybersecurity incidents, incident response, digital forensic investigations, information security
programs, cybersecurity governance, and data protection. His work includes analyzing forensic
evidence to determine the circumstances, chronology, and scope of digital events. It also includes
evaluating whether electronic content can be authenticated and reliably attributed to its source, and
explaining complex technical findings to courts and counsel.

Mr. Garrie is an Adjunct Professor at Harvard Extension School and has taught at Rutgers,
Cardozo, and UConn Law Schools. A prolific author on cybersecurity, incident response, digital
forensics, and ediscovery, he regularly trains judges, counsel, and organizations.

Some of Daniel Garrie's significant achievements are listed below:
•   Appointed or served as forensic neutral, digital forensics, or technical expert witness or court-appointed
    expert in over 100 disputes in state and federal courts.
•   Recognized by the American Bar Association and the Federal Judiciary as a subject matter expert on
    digital forensics and cybersecurity controls and systems.
•   Co-authored Understanding Software, the Internet, Mobile Computing, and the Cloud. A guide for
    Judges, published by the Federal Judicial Center in 2015. Authored six books, including several books
    on cybersecurity including Cybersecurity & the Courthouse: Safeguarding the Judicial Process
    (Wiley); Law Firm Cybersecurity (ABA); and eDiscovery Dispute Resolution (Westlegal Ed).
•   Presented at 600+ seminars to numerous judges, lawyers, and students across the globe on a variety of
    topics such as digital forensic investigations, incident response, cybersecurity, and ediscovery.
•   Co-inventor of digital forensic patents: 10546129, 10528738, 9990498, 9990497.
•   Co-authored the JAMS Artificial Intelligence Dispute Resolution Rules, establishing one of the first
    comprehensive frameworks for the resolution of AI-related legal disputes.

 Judge Segal’s experience as a U.S. Magistrate Judge for the Central District of California, including four
 years as Chief Magistrate Judge, provides her with a comprehensive perspective on the dynamics of
 federal litigation. Over nearly two decades on the bench, she presided over numerous trials, evidentiary
 hearings, motions, and discovery conferences across a broad range of subject areas. She served as a
 settlement judge in hundreds of matters involving business and insurance disputes, intellectual property
 and patent claims, employment and civil rights cases, and complex tort and class actions.

 her among neutrals. She has handled a wide array of disputes involving copyright and trademark
 infringement, patent litigation, False Claims Act and Medicare reimbursement actions, and class actions.
 She has also served as a special master and discovery referee in high-value cases involving product
 liability, mass tort, and insurance coverage issues.

 Before her judicial appointment, Judge Segal spent twelve years as an Assistant United States Attorney in

the Civil Division of the Los Angeles U.S. Attorney’s Oﬃce. She handled complex contract, employment,
civil rights, and tort cases, and also brought consumer and civil rights enforcement actions on behalf of
the Department of Justice. As Chief of Civil Appeals from 1999 to 2002, she oversaw the oﬃce’s appellate
practice and supervised numerous signiﬁcant cases before the Ninth Circuit. Earlier in her career, she
practiced at Dewey Ballantine and Adams, Duque & Hazeltine, where she represented clients in business

Judge Segal holds a Juris Doctor from Cornell Law School and a Bachelor of Arts, cum laude, from

                                                Hon. Karen S. Crawford

 “My goal is to help you reach resolution. That means speaking directly with
  the parties, addressing the real costs of continued litigation, financial and
   otherwise, and staying with the case as long as it takes to get it settled. I
   understand the litigation process, evaluate and weigh positions asserted,
identify what is actually driving the dispute, and help people make clear-eyed
decisions. That is what I have done my entire career, both as a litigator and as
                           a U.S. Magistrate Judge.”


 BIOGRAPHY
 Hon. Karen S. Crawford (Ret.) joins Signature Resolution with a career built in equal measure on the
 complexity of high-stakes litigation and the vision and discipline to help parties resolve their disputes. A
 former U.S. Magistrate Judge with fourteen years on the federal bench and a litigation career spanning the
 Department of Justice, the U.S. Attorney’s Oﬃce, and law ﬁrms with a national practice, Judge Crawford
 brings ﬁrsthand knowledge of how complex disputes arise, how they are litigated, and how they are
 resolved. Her frank approach is grounded in a career spent understanding the needs of diverse clients,
 from individual claimants to multinational corporations, and assisting them in balancing the risks and
 costs of litigation against the likelihood of success so they can make well-informed, strategic settlement
 decisions.

 Her commitment to direct, honest engagement deﬁnes Judge Crawford’s mediation style. She questions
 positions asserted, pressing counsel to trace the path from their arguments to their desired outcome, and
 structures her sessions to ensure every party in the room understands where they stand and the litigation
           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR            Document 3571-5         Filed 10/15/26      Page 3 of 5

challenges they face. She addresses the costs of prolonged litigation candidly, walking parties through the
ﬁnancial realities associated with ongoing depositions, written discovery, and anticipated disputes, making
the stakes of unresolved and time-consuming conﬂicts concrete rather than abstract. When progress
stalls, she makes clear that her role is ongoing until resolution is reached and encourages parties to
reconvene whenever they are ready to adjust their settlement strategies.

Appointed to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California in March 2012, Judge Crawford
presided over a broad range of federal civil matters and was responsible for scheduling and managing
pretrial proceedings and conducting settlement conferences for a diverse and high-volume docket. She
assisted litigants ranging from corporate defendants managing complex, multiparty exposure matters to
cases brought by individual plaintiﬀs for whom the outcome was deeply personal. She developed a
precise read on where cases were strong and what positions were vulnerable and separately shared her
perspective with all parties. Judge Crawford’s ability to speak plainly about the likelihood of success,
litigation risks and costs, and potential outcomes enabled her to bring parties together to reach
resolution.

Judge Crawford developed her mediation skills throughout her career as a litigator, where case resolution
was an essential consideration in all of her cases. During her early career as a Trial Attorney in the Civil
Division’s Torts Branch of the U.S. Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., she traveled around the
country trying cases on behalf of the United States in mass tort multidistrict litigation ﬁled pursuant to the
National Swine Flu Immunization Program of 1976, P.L. 94-380, 90 Stat. 1113 (August 12, 1976). She
continued to defend these cases after leaving Washington, D.C., and joining the U.S. Attorney’s Oﬃce in
San Diego as an Assistant U.S. Attorney. There, her practice expanded to representing the United States in
cases involving constitutional torts, personal injury and wrongful death, vaccine litigation, road design,
medical malpractice, and a broad range of other civil matters.

Upon moving to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 1991, Judge Crawford entered private practice and later
opened and managed the ﬁrst West Coast oﬃce for her ﬁrm in San Diego in 2005. Her private practice
expanded to representing clients in commercial disputes in both state and federal courts, including
matters involving breach of contract, theft of trade secrets, unfair business practices, and intellectual
property disputes. She also served as national counsel to an international latex glove manufacturer in the
defense of hundreds of cases in both federal multidistrict and state coordinated products liability
proceedings. Defending these cases across multiple jurisdictions throughout the United States required
Judge Crawford to build a cohesive team of lawyers and experts to ensure consistent strategies and
positions were asserted on behalf of her client. She gained a keen understanding of her client’s goals by
working with in-house counsel on a daily basis as they coordinated eﬀective defenses. That work gave her
a sophisticated understanding of client needs, how to assess litigation risks, and what it takes to move
large-scale disputes toward resolution. Judge Crawford went on to lead the litigation group at Duane
Morris in San Diego in 2005 before her appointment as a U.S. Magistrate Judge.

Throughout her career, Judge Crawford has been actively involved in her legal community, particularly
through organizations that aﬀord her the opportunity to mentor law students and young lawyers. One
such organization is the American Inns of Court, which is dedicated to promoting civility, ethics, and
professionalism in the practice of law. Judge Crawford joined an Inn of Court chapter early in her career
           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR            Document 3571-5         Filed 10/15/26      Page 4 of 5

and has continued her involvement to date as a Master, Board Member, and President of several
chapters. On a national level, she participated on the American Inns of Court Foundation Board of

Judge Crawford’s sustained commitment to the legal community as a practitioner and judicial oﬃcer, and
her substantial work to improve the civility of legal practice, also drive her eﬀorts to assist counsel and

1        I.       INTRODUCTION
2              Plaintiff Charleston County School District (“CCSD”) respectfully submits this motion in limine
3    to exclude evidence concerning allegations of mismanagement or compliance issues relating to federal
4    COVID-Relief (ESSER) funds. Such evidence, including investigative reports, complaints, legal filings
5    and media coverage, has no bearing on whether Defendants’ social media platforms caused Plaintiff’s
6    harm. Even if the Court determines the evidence is relevant, exclusion remains warranted because its
7    minimal probative value is substantially outweighed by the risk of unfair prejudice and will require the
8    time-consuming presentation of evidence to address the wholly collateral issue.
9        II.      BACKGROUND
10             In 2024, CCSD paid $3 million in overdue charges to a vendor that provided services to improve
11   reading levels in two areas of the district, Hollywood and Ravenel. Valerie Nava, Details emerge of $3M
12   Charleston Co. schools pain in COVID-relief fund debacle; director fired, POST AND COURIER (July 21,
13   2024),            https://www.postandcourier.com/education-lab/ccsd-charleston-esser-3-million-director-
14   fired/article_baa9b07c-447a-11ef-982f-6f49ee044448.html. The payments were supposed to be covered
15   by federal funds from the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief plan (“ESSER”), a federal
16   program providing pandemic relief aid to state and local education agencies. But the District’s executive
17   director of federal programs, John Cobb, mishandled the necessary steps in the procurement process and
18   failed to obtain this funding. Id.
19             The District hired an outside law firm to conduct an investigation. Id. In July 2024, the firm
20   released its findings, concluding that the District’s inability to use ESSER funds was due to a failure to
21   follow specific procurement processes. Id. The report further found that Cobb “demonstrated poor
22   leadership,” and “a lack of planning and oversight,” and acted negligently, costing the district over $3
23   million. Id. Immediately upon the report’s release, the District fired Cobb. Id.
24             Following his termination, Cobb accused the District of mismanaging the funds and claimed its
25   superintendent, Dr. Anita Huggins, created a hostile work environment. Id. In July 2024, Cobb filed a
26   complaint against the District under the federal False Claims Act; the lawsuit remains ongoing. Valerie
27   Nava, Former Charleston public schools exec sues district over alleged misspending of $3M in federal
28
                                                          1

                                           TO EXCLUDE REFERENCE TO ALLEGATIONS OF MISMANAGEMENT OF ESSER FUNDS

1    funds, POST AND COURIER (Jan. 23, 2026), https://www.postandcourier.com/education-lab/former-
2    charleston-exec-sues-school-district/article_25b3390c-de73-4860-89c0-9ede8dca0569.html.             In 2026,
3    Cobb’s complaint was unsealed by the Department of Justice when it declined to intervene but allowed
4    the case to proceed. Id. CCSD has denied Cobb’s allegations. Colt Yeargin, Former Charleston Co. School
5    District employee files federal lawsuit over alleged fund misuse, LIVE 5 NEWS (Jan. 23, 2026),
6    https://www.live5news.com/2026/01/23/former-charleston-co-school-district-employee-files-federal-
7    lawsuit-over-alleged-fund-misuse/. During a meet and confer with CCSD about anticipated motions in
8    limine, Defendants indicated they would seek to introduce at trial the evidence Plaintiff seeks to exclude
9    here.
10      III.      LEGAL STANDARD
11             Evidence is admissible under Fed. R. Evid. 402 if it is relevant, meaning it “has any tendency to
12   make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence” and “the fact is of consequence
13   in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid. 401. Relevant evidence may nonetheless be excluded “if its
14   probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of one or more of the following: unfair prejudice,
15   confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative
16   evidence.” Fed. R. Evid. 403.
17      IV.       ARGUMENT
18             Federal Rule of Evidence 402 precludes Defendants from using evidence regarding allegations of
19   mismanagement related to ESSER funding, as such evidence is irrelevant. Even assuming the evidence is
20   relevant, the Court should nonetheless exclude it under Rule 403 because it is unfairly prejudicial and will
21   require the time-consuming presentation of evidence with little probative value.
22                a. Evidence Concerning the Alleged Mismanagement of ESSER Funds is Inadmissible
                     Because it is Irrelevant.
23

24             Evidence is relevant if it makes a material fact more or less probable. Fed. R. Evid. 402; Fed. R.
25   Evid. 401. In other words, evidence is considered relevant if it has a meaningful relation to a fact at issue
26   in the case. See United States v. Curtin, 489 F.3d 935, 943 (9th Cir. 2007) (citing Advisory Committee’s
27   Notes on Fed. R. Evid. 401). The inquiry into the relevancy of evidence is “fact based and depends on
28
                                                           2
                                                                                    PLAINTIFF’S MOTION IN LIMINE #1
                                            TO EXCLUDE REFERENCE TO ALLEGATIONS OF MISMANAGEMENT OF ESSER FUNDS
                                                                           IN CHARLESTON COUNTY SCHOOL DISTRICT
           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR              Document 3575         Filed 10/16/26       Page 4 of 10



1    many factors, including how closely related the evidence is to the plaintiff’s circumstances and theory of
2    the case.” Sprint/United Management Co. v. Mendelsohn, 552 U.S. 379, 388 (2008); see, e.g., Pham v.
3    Bast, No. 17-CV-04194-WHO, 2023 WL 4053415, at *2 (N.D. Cal. June 15, 2023). Evidence related to
4    CCSD’s management of ESSER funds is unrelated to the issues in the present case and is therefore
5    irrelevant.
6               Plaintiff raises a single count of negligence against Defendants. Specifically, as laid out in the
7    District’s proposed jury instructions, Plaintiff alleges that the Defendants breached their duty to use
8    ordinary care by (1) “not providing the warnings that a reasonably prudent, competent company concerned
9    with user safety would have provided”; (2) “designing, operating, and/or marketing their social media
10   platforms in a way that caused students to engage in problematic use, compulsive use, and/or become
11   addicted”; (3) “deliberately targeting school-aged children, when the Defendants knew or reasonably
12   should have foreseen the impact that doing so would have on schools”; and (4) “not designing, operating,
13   and/or marketing their social media platforms as a reasonably prudent, safety conscious, and competent
14   company would have done.” Dkt. 2681 at 46. In their discussions with Plaintiff, Defendants have been
15   unable to articulate a plausible connection between any of these elements of the negligence cause of action
16   and the timeliness of the District’s use of federal pandemic funds. Allegations of procurement
17   mismanagement plainly have nothing to do with whether Defendants provided safety warnings, whether
18   they operated their platforms in an unsafe way, whether they targeted students, or whether they designed
19   their platforms as a reasonable prudent company would have done.
20              That connection is also facially nonexistent with respect to the causation element of Plaintiff’s
21   negligence claim (whether “Defendants’ failure to use ordinary care was a substantial factor in causing
22   harm to Charleston,” id.). While Defendants’ experts discuss COVID-19 pandemic and its purported
23   impact on school systems, Defendants have proffered no expert testimony purporting to establish that the
24   District’s alleged mismanagement of COVID-era federal funds is an alternative cause of the District’s
25   injury.1
26

27   1
      Through this motion, the District does not seek to bar Defendants from raising the COVID-19
28   pandemic more generally as an alternative cause of the District’s injuries.

1           Finally, any assertion that this evidence is relevant to damages is unavailing. The damages element
2    concerns whether the district “incurred expenses related to the harm Defendants’ social media platforms
3    caused.” Id. at 47. It does not concern whether, at an impressionistic level, a jury thinks CCSD will use
4    an award competently. Importantly, even if that were a valid consideration, CCSD and independent
5    investigators concluded that the mishandling of ESSER funds was attributable to the negligence of a single

19       I.      INTRODUCTION
20            Plaintiff moves pursuant to Federal Rules of Evidence 401, 402, and 403 to exclude any
21    testimony or documents concerning allegations of specific instances of racial discrimination,
22    hostility, or racist conduct involving students or personnel within Charleston County School
23    District (“Charleston”). These collateral events concern highly prejudicial incidents that either pre-
24    date the relevant time period of Plaintiff’s damages or are disconnected from Charleston’s theory
25    of harm and/or Defendants’ alternative causation theories or affirmative defenses.
26            Plaintiff specifically seeks to exclude evidence or argument concerning the following
27    incidents and the underlying events giving rise thereto (together, the “Incidents”):
28

 1                   a 2008 U.S. Department of Education Office for Civil Rights investigation in

 4                    Black neighborhoods;

 8                   a 2017 lawsuit alleging racial discrimination at certain schools;

 9                   2021 allegations of racially discriminatory hiring practices in the facilities

10                    department;

11                   a 2021 incident where students displayed the Confederate flag in violation of the

12                    student code of conduct;

13                   a 2022 lawsuit alleging that the Charleston curriculum used critical race theory and

14                    was thus racially discriminatory; and

15                   2022 allegations of racially discriminatory employment practices at a high school.

16             The admission of evidence related to these Incidents would not make any material fact

17    concerning Defendants’ platform design or causation of Plaintiff’s claimed damages more or less

18    probable. Any alleged probative value is substantially outweighed by danger of unfair prejudice,

19    would mislead the jury, and would lead to unnecessary “mini-trials” on collateral issues. The Court

20    should exclude this evidence under Rules 401, 402, and 403.

23    “has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence” and

24    “the fact is of consequence in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid. 401. Relevant evidence may

25    nonetheless be excluded “if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of one or

26    more of the following: unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay,

27    wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.” Fed. R. Evid. 403.

                          ritual defamation case
                                    Post & Courier (Charleston, SC)

Length: 451 words

Byline: Jenna Schiferl ; , jschiferl@postandcourier.com
Highlight: The South Carolina Court of Appeals ruled Wednesday to uphold the dismissal of a
defamation lawsuit involving a former Academic Magnet High School football coach and a
controversial post-game ritual.

Body


The S.C. Court of Appeals ruled Wednesday to uphold the dismissal of a defamation lawsuit
involving a former Academic Magnet High School football coach and a controversial post-game
ritual.

At issue were two editorials published by Charleston City Paper in 2014 about Academic
Magnet's former football coach Eugene "Bud" Walpole and the football team's victory ritual in
which players chanted and smashed watermelons with caricature-like faces painted on them.

Football coach sues over alleged racial discrimination

"We're very pleased with the decision. We think it was the right one," said Wallace Lightsey, an
attorney for Jones Street Publishers, owner and publisher of Charleston City Paper.

The football tradition was criticized by many for perpetuating racist stereotypes against African
Americans, and it garnered intense media attention from local and national outlets.

In November 2014, members of the football team filed a defamation complaint against Jones
Street Publishers, Charleston County School District, Atlanta-based diversity consultant Kevin
Clayton and his firm Axxis Consulting.

A month later, Walpole also filed a similar defamation complaint against the same defendants,
and both cases were eventually combined in 2015.

The lawsuit argued that the articles implied that Walpole and football team were racist.

A year later, the Court of Common Pleas ruled that the reporting and editorials were protected
by law and didn't defame the plaintiffs. Walpole's attorneys appealed the decision.

Judge rules in favor of Charleston City Paper in Academic Magnet defamation suit
         Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3576-3         Filed 10/16/26      Page 3 of 3
                                                                                               Page 2 of 2
        SC Court of Appeals upholds dismissal of Academic Magnet watermelon ritual defamation case

After almost three years of legal back-and-forth, the Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal
Wednesday.

"We respectfully disagree with the opinion," said William Barnes, an attorney for Walpole and
the football players. "We feel being called a racist (expletive) is defamatory," referring to one of
the editorials published by Charleston City Paper.

The opinion found the factual statements in the articles were protected by the fair report
privilege and the opinions published were protected under the First Amendment. The opinion
also said the proof of injury to reputation was not shown, and it was not shown that the
defendants "acted with actual malice."

Noel Mermer, then-publisher of Charleston City Paper, called it a "Great day for the First
Amendment" in an email to The Post and Courier.

Walpole and the football players' attorneys could seek a rehearing, and if that's denied, appeal
further to the South Carolina Supreme Court.

Football coach sues over alleged racial discrimination

"As far as going forward, that's something that we're going to be talking to our clients about and
making a decision on," Barnes said.

Highlight: Lucy Beckham High School leaders are working to address cultural issues in the

Body


MOUNT PLEASANT - Lucy Beckham High School leaders are working to address cultural
issues in the school after a student flew a Confederate flag from a truck during a spirit week
event.

The school kicked off its spirit week Oct. 18 with a 'Merica Monday theme during which students
were encouraged to wear patriotic outfits. After the school day began, one of the students
arrived with a Confederate flag flying from their truck, Principal Anna Dassing said in a
statement to The Post and Courier.

When school officials discovered the flag they disciplined the student in accordance with the
district's contraband rules in the Student Code of Conduct, which prohibits students from
possessing or viewing "items considered to be unsuitable for school or school related activities."

District spokesman Andrew Pruitt was unable to share specifics on the student's punishment,
citing privacy concerns. It is considered a level one offense where the maximum punishment is
an in-school suspension.

The school is also working to create a focus group composed of students, staff and parents that
will discuss race, equity, inclusion, and other issues facing young adults.

Lucy Beckham High becomes first school in SC to offer Coast Guard JROTC program

The focus group comes after a number of parents sent emails and left messages with school
officials expressing their concerns that the 'Merica themed spirit day and Confederate flag
incident are signs of a worsening culture at the school.

Vanessa Hinson received a text from her son during the school day on Oct. 18 with a picture of
the flag flying from the truck and the message "this is going on in our parking lot." After Hinson
picked her son up from school, he told her that the flag had stayed up for most of the day and
students were sharing videos of it on social media.
         Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR            Document 3576-4          Filed 10/16/26       Page 3 of 4
                                                                                               Page 2 of 3
                  Lucy Beckham High parents call for action after Confederate flag incident

The flag was not the only divisive incident that occurred. Other parents heard about a number of
students who arrived to the school that day wearing Confederate flag paraphernalia. They were
disciplined for violating the school's dress code.

Charleston County School District encourages in-person learning as case numbers drop

"These students were obviously sending social media messages out on this subject, but nobody
went to administration and raised it with them, which means there's not a culture of safety that
people know when they should or that they can securely or safely report an incident," Hinson
said.

Hinson is not the only parent concerned about Lucy Beckham students feeling unsafe. Susan
Carr, who has a son at the school, learned about the incident from a fellow parent who had
reached out to her to discuss potentially taking action.

The incident left her feeling worried about what her son is experiencing at school and whether
he feels comfortable advocating for himself.

"A culture at a school comes top down," Carr said.

Other parents were frustrated with the school's response to the incident. Although many
members of the Lucy Beckham community knew about the flag by the end of the day on Oct. 18,
the school has yet to officially address it in its messaging to parents.

Thousands of South Carolina students expected to sign pledge against gun violence

In an Oct. 25 newsletter sent to parents, Dassing reiterated the school's dedication to diversity,
equity and inclusion and mentioned that students will be participating in town halls and classes
to reaffirm the school's expectations.

"In our Town Halls, our team will reiterate that, while we strive to provide a space where
students can express themselves as they explore who they are, we will not tolerate acts of
bullying, harassment, intimidation, hateful speech or displays, and/or apparel that has the
potential of causing a disruption," she wrote.

Though the newsletter gave parents some reassurance, some wanted to hear the administration
directly address the incident with them. Rebecca Byrd, whose two children are sophomores at
Lucy Beckham, pointed out that when a child makes a mistake they are taught to admit to it,
apologize, and say how they plan on correcting the harm done going forward.

"That's all I ask from the school, to do those things publicly," Byrd said.

Lucy Beckham has been around for two years.

      Charleston County School District bans images of Confederate flag
                                    Post & Courier (Charleston, SC)
                                        August 18, 2015 Tuesday

Copyright 2015 The Post and Courier All Rights Reserved

Section: 01,A; Pg. 1
Length: 519 words

Byline: bopete@postandcourier.com

Body


After months of racially charged violence, including the killing of nine Emanuel AME Church
members, as well as the disputed removal of the Confederate flag from Statehouse grounds
spurred by that horror, the Charleston County School District has banned students from
displaying the flag emblem on campus.

The decision was announced on a plain white page inserted into the district s Student Code of
Conduct for 2015-16. The page reads in part that in light of a year marred with racially divisive
and tragic events students would be prohibited from wearing on campus clothing, jewelry or
other apparel bearing the image of the Confederate flag. It goes on to add that the image can t
be displayed prominently on vehicles driven to school.

Students will be asked to remove the emblem and discipline will be on a case-by-case basis, the
page says. Asked for comment, a spokesman for the district replied with a statement restating
the white page. It was a staff decision, said Daniel Head, the spokesman.

School board chairwoman Cindy Bohn Coats could not be reached for comment.

Dylann Roof, the man accused of the Emanuel AME shooting, had posted online a manifesto of
white supremacist beliefs and photographs showing him visiting historic slave sites and waving
the Confederate battle flag, federal authorities have said.

Neither Berkeley County nor Dorchester County District 2 schools have discussed a similar
policy, its spokespeople said. Both systems rely on a standard school district policy that gives
principals or administrators authority to remove student items or behavior deemed disruptive,
they said. Charleston County Schools also has that policy.

The prohibition didn t appear to stir much reaction from parents on the first day. There were few,
if any, social media postings. At least one parent said it was a good move. A critic of the schools
racial policies agreed.

Wearing or displaying the Confederate flag would be disruptive at school, said Sarah Johnson,
who has a daughter at Wando High School.
         Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR          Document 3576-5          Filed 10/16/26         Page 3 of 3
                                                                                               Page 2 of 2
                    Charleston County School District bans images of Confederate flag

 It s a decent thing to do. It helps at least show in good faith how the community is trying to
come together rather than stay divisive, said the Rev. John Brown, of Mt. Zion AME Church in
Charleston. He has been part of a group protesting what it considers racial bias on the school
board in the hiring of Superintendent Gerrita Postlewait and other recent decisions. I just hope it
s not a token rule.

The prohibition comes amid a surge of demonstrations in support of the flag and its heritage,
including a display of the flags Sunday at the Charleston Battery and on vehicles around the
Lowcountry. More than 170 pro-flag rallies have been held across the country since the
Emanuel AME Church shooting in June, The Washington Post has reported.

Requests for comment from Confederacy heritage supporters weren t returned. One person
asked said people with children in the schools did not want to comment for attribution because
they were afraid of being ostracized.

Andrew Knapp contributed to this story. Reach Bo Petersen at 937-5744, @bopete on twitter or

                                    Post & Courier (Charleston, SC)
                                      December 1, 2022 Thursday

Copyright 2022 The Post and Courier All Rights Reserved

Section: A; news/crime; news/local state news; news; Pg. 3
Length: 725 words

Byline: Maura Turcotte ; , mturcotte@postandcourier.com
Highlight: The S.C. Freedom Caucus is suing Charleston County School District over claims
schools are indoctrinating students to discriminate against others.

Body


A faction of S.C. House Republican lawmakers are suing Charleston County School District over
claims its schools are teaching critical race theory.

The lawsuit, filed on Nov. 28 by the S.C. Freedom Caucus, claims the district violated state law
by using state funds for lessons the group says teach students to discriminate against others.
The caucus argued lessons about how White people benefit from structural racism infringe on
constitutional rights and state laws protecting students from discrimination.

The lawsuit's claims echo those of the other lawsuit that the Freedom Caucus filed against the
Lexington 1 school district in mid-November.

Curriculums that allegedly teach critical race theory have been under attack across the country.
In Georgia, one educator was pushed out of her role in the Cherokee County School District
before she even started over fears she was going to impose critical race theory curriculum on
schools, and school districts in both Tennessee and Connecticut have been sued over the
concept. Critical race theory is the academic framework that looks at racism embedded in public
policy and legal institutions in the United States, and is typically taught in graduate level
courses.

Charleston County School District is examining the claims, according to Andy Pruitt, CCSD
spokesman.

"We are consulting our legal team to ensure we take the appropriate next steps to resolve this,"
he said in a statement.

The Freedom Caucus, which formed in April 2022, is made up of hardline conservatives. The
S.C. law cited, which was inserted into the state budget last year, prohibits state money from
being used to teach students or train instructors, administrators and staff in concepts that fall
under "partisanship curriculum."
         Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR         Document 3576-6        Filed 10/16/26   Page 3 of 4
                                                                                      Page 2 of 3
                           Right-wing legislators sue CCSD over CRT claims

Hardline faction of SC House Republicans sues Lexington schools over CRT claims

These ideas include teaching that one race or sex is inherently superior to another, and that
people, whether consciously or unconsciously, are inherently oppressive because of their race
or sex.

Much of the lawsuit focused on EL Education, a New York-based nonprofit that provides
curricula and training to schools across the country. EL Education's website lists Charleston as
one of its district partners.

In the lawsuit, the Freedom Caucus claimed EL Education is "obsessed with race" and included,
among other points, details from EL Education's website in which the organization outlines its
commitment to equity and anti-racism. The website states the organization views "education as
a powerful engine for disrupting structural racism."

In response to the claims, EL Education CEO Scott Hartl stood by his organization's learning
services, which he called based in the science of learning, aligned with South Carolina's
standards and validated by third-party research.

"We're disappointed that the South Carolina Freedom Caucus will divert public education
resources for political aims which are not in the best interest of children. EL Education stands
with the Charleston County School District in working to ensure that students have access to
high-quality learning opportunities," he said.

Right-wing legislators admit editing audio used in Fox News report attacking SC schools

The Freedom Caucus first attacked Lexington 1 and its partnership with EL Education in late
October. The caucus released an edited audio recording of an EL Education employee in which
she is heard saying the organization's curriculum has been developed to be "inclusive of
culturally relevant teaching."

The caucus claimed it was proof of "liberal indoctrination" of students, and the recording sparked
a Fox News report.

Hartl told The Post and Courier at the time that the employee's responses were "deliberately
twisted into a false and crudely edited narrative."

Still, the audio recording provided the basis of the Freedom Caucus' lawsuit in Lexington 1.

At the Nov. 16 announcement for the Lexington 1 lawsuit, Rep. Adam Morgan of Greenville
County, chairman of the caucus, said the recording "clearly revealed there are in fact people
coming into South Carolina being paid by districts to teach teachers how to incorporate the very
things that violate state standards and state law and incorporate them into their classroom."

Section: A; news/crime; news/local state news; news; Pg. 3
Length: 1480 words

Byline: Hillary Flynn ; , hflynn@postandcourier.com
Highlight: The Nov. 8 election increased the influence of controversial parents' rights group Moms for Liberty.

Body


Moms for Liberty, a conservative parents' rights organization, emerged as a growing political power in South
Carolina education this election cycle.

The group is known for speaking out against social-emotional learning curriculums, LGBTQ education and any
semblance of teaching critical race theory in K-12 public schools.

It made national headlines for a slew of controversies ranging from the New Hampshire chapter tweeting that they
would give a $500 reward to anyone who caught a teacher using critical race theory in their lessons, to a group of
Florida members telling MSNBC in an interview that there should be separate classes for LGBTQ and cisgender
students. They have also been associated with efforts to ban books from public school libraries, many of which
discuss LGBTQ issues and Black history.

School board candidates endorsed by the group won the majority of seats in Charleston and Berkeley counties, and
made gains in regions across the state on Nov. 8.

To an extent, this mirrors broader political trends. While the red wave heavily touted by conservative politicians
didn't sweep the country, Republican politicians were successful in many areas of South Carolina. In Charleston
County, a competitive, historically purple region, they flipped two county council seats erasing the narrowly held 5-4
Democratic majority.

Their increasing political power in South Carolina has some education community members concerned about how
their political views will impact children's education, particularly children from historically marginalized communities.

"We need to recognize that this group and some groups like them are targeting transgender people and other
members of the LGBTQ+ community, and that's very harmful," said Kristen French, a current CCSD school board
member who did not seek reelection. "In terms of that, it's so important to remember that part of a school and what
we want students to learn is how to work with others who are different from them, and be respectful and kind to
those that are different from them."

Tiffany Justice and Tina Descovich, two former school board members, started Moms for Liberty in Florida in 2021.
They both felt that parents didn't get enough voice in public schools and that their needs weren't being taken into
consideration.
           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR                 Document 3578-3              Filed 10/16/26    Page 3 of 4
                    Controversial parents' rights group Moms for Liberty increases influence in SC

This belief was exacerbated during the coronavirus pandemic when school districts nationwide switched to remote
learning, and many of those that continued teaching in-person mandated that students and staff wear masks while
in the building.

"I'm a parent, I get to direct medical care for my children," Justice said.

The organization now has 240 chapters across 42 states and over 100,000 members. There are 16 chapters across
South Carolina from Charleston in the Lowcountry, to Lexington in the Midlands and Florence in the Pee Dee and
Pickens in the Upstate.

The organization's objectives include getting parents' rights law passed in every state and eliminate critical race
theory from public school curriculums.

Critical race theory is an academic framework that examines the racism embedded in public policy and legal
institutions, and is typically taught in law schools not in grades K-12.

The group also wants to get rid of social-emotional learning, soft skills many schools are now teaching children to
help them with self-control and personal interaction. Justice believes these curriculums are a waste of school
financial resources and time. She thinks schools should be more focused on academics. Studies have shown
incorporating social-emotional learning into curriculums improves school safety and students' mental health,
something that has suffered greatly since the pandemic.

The organization also wants to push for children to read books they consider age appropriate, as well as ones they
feel aren't violating state and federal obscenity laws. Justice likened it to the age restrictions on movies and video
games.

"If it has explicit graphic sexual material, then it has no place in a school," Justice said.

When asked about the New Hampshire chapter's tweet, Justice said the wording could have been better, but if
critical race theory wasn't being taught in classrooms then it shouldn't be an issue. In regards to the MSNBC
interview with the group of Florida members, she said the women didn't believe that LGBTQ students should be
taught in separate classes, but if they were struggling with their sexuality or gender identity the teacher should
speak to them about it one-on-one or in small groups rather than discussing LGBTQ issues with the whole class.

During the election, candidates endorsed by Moms for Liberty's local chapters won five of the nine school board
seats in Charleston County and six of the eight in Berkeley. They made smaller gains in other counties, adding an
endorsed member to school boards in Beaufort, Dorchester 2, Kershaw and elsewhere.

Candidates endorsed by political parties or special interest groups are not beholden to their beliefs. In school board
races, some candidates earn nominations from multiple groups. In Charleston County, two candidates were by
endorsed by the county Republican and Democratic parties as well as the Charleston Coalition for Kids, a group
that formed in 2018 to recruit and support certain school board candidates.

Tara Wood, the chair of Charleston's Moms for Liberty, said the group first started coming together 15 months ago.
She was at a meeting in Mount Pleasant where an education expert spoke about critical race theory. After the
meeting, Wood and approximately 10 other women went up to the speaker and talked about critical race theory for
three hours. Wood said the conversation was cordial. She got the 10 women's numbers and sent out a group text
asking them if they wanted to meet for coffee sometime.

They met informally for several times discussing problems they had with education in Charleston County. Wood
agreed with Moms for Liberty's philosophies and started looking into opening a local chapter. Wood hosted the first
official Moms for Liberty meeting in August 2021.

About 60 people showed up. Now she said over 300 people sometimes attend their meetings.

                    Controversial parents' rights group Moms for Liberty increases influence in SC

Regarding local issues, the Charleston chapter is against the school district's new governance model where the
board's administrative duties will be passed to the superintendent so the board can focus more on student
academics. It is also against executive sessions, or discussion the school board can have that are not open to the
public.

Andy Pruitt, a spokesman for CCSD, said in a statement that Superintendent Don Kennedy will work with board
members to improve students' academics in the district.

"CCSD is optimistic that the development of the student outcome governance framework goals will result in
significant improvement in student outcomes and that continued efforts toward the Board-adopted goals will impact
the lives of many for years to come," he said.

The Charleston chapter's philosophy deviates slightly from its parent organization's beliefs on critical race theory.
Woods does not think that critical race theory is being taught in schools but that its tenants have trickled down into
K-12 curriculums.

"Anytime you make the narrative 'White man bad, dark man good' that's CRT and that's horrible," she said.

She is against LGBTQ education in schools and social-emotional learning curriculums, which she also believes
saps schools financial resources and class time where students could be spent learning core academics.

"What does it matter if a teacher figures out a kid is gay if he can't read?" she asked.

Keith Grybowski and Ed Kelly, two candidates Moms for Liberty endorsed who won their elections, both said that
they support parents having more voice in their children's education. They are divided over other issues, such as
the new school governance model, and are focused on students' academic performance and teacher retention.

Kelly, who was also endorsed by the Charleston County Republican Party, said that he doesn't support the new
governance model and that he is doing research into social-emotional learning.

"The job of schools is to teach reading, writing and arithmetic," he said. "If we have time to teach kids how to deal
with feelings that's terrific, but that's not our core directive."

Grybowski said that he will not second guess what the current board did in regards to the school governance model
and said that the first issue the new board will have to address is hiring a new superintendent. (Kennedy's position
was always meant to be temporary.) He added that his main goal as a board member is to improve teacher
retention.

"Without teachers, many students will not have the one-on-one literacy support they need if we are going to close
the gap," he said.

Highlight: South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster chastised members of Charleston County School Board after

Body


South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster chastised members of Charleston County School Board after a bipartisan
slew of lawmakers accused them of violating state open-meeting laws.

The board held a discussion about suspending Superintendent Eric Gallien in a closed-door executive session
during a Sept. 25 board meeting. When the board returned to the open meeting, they voted 5-4 to place Gallien on
paid administrative leave as a staff complaint against him is investigated. He has been on the job for three months.

State Rep. Joe Bustos, the Republican chairman of the Charleston legislative delegation, on Oct. 1 wrote McMaster
to ask that he have the state Office of Inspector General investigate as to whether the five members of the school
board violated South Carolina's open-meetings law after having a discussion about suspending the superintendent
in executive session.

Charleston lawmakers ask Gov. McMaster, attorney general to investigate school board

The following day, Wendell Gilliard, D-Charleston, published a letter calling on Attorney General Alan Wilson to
launch an investigation into the actions of the five school board members. He noted the faction was supported by
Moms for Liberty. The conservative parents' rights group is known for opposing LGBTQ education and critical race
theory, among other matters.

On Oct. 3, McMaster told reporters outside of the Statehouse in Columbia that conversations outside of the public
eye not only cause members of the community to lose confidence in their school boards, but also business leaders,
who may begin to second-guess their decision to move their businesses and employees into the district.

SC school districts on track to meet $3.3B relief funds deadline. But what comes next?

"The school district needs to follow the law," McMaster said. "The Freedom of Information Act is very clear.
Everybody ought to follow the law when they're asked questions that fall within the ambit of the Freedom of
Information Act; they ought to give the information out and give it out fairly quickly. It does not look to me like the
school board has done that."

Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle asked McMaster, the state inspector general and the S.C. attorney general
to investigate the board's conduct.

"If it gets worse," McMaster said about opening a state investigation. "I don't think we're at that point yet."

Bustos told The Post and Courier that he still believes an investigation is in order.

"I still believe an inquiry needs to be done, but he is the governor," Bustos said. "We must wait to see what happens
with the school board."

Gilliard called McMaster's actions "disappointing" but not surprising, and said he has never shown much care for
South Carolina's public schools, as evidence by them consistently scoring near the bottom of national rankings.

The five board members who voted to suspend Gallien - Pamela McKinney, Carlotte Bailey, Keith Grybowski, Ed
Kelley and Leah Whatley - said in an Oct. 3 statement that the board is fractured to such a degree that their
differences in opinion are being used to falsely villainize certain CCSD board members.

"We have remained largely silent in the past week, hoping our colleagues would come to conduct discussions that
promote understanding and empathy rather than exacerbate divisions," they said. "Following yesterday's press
conference and various social media posts over the last week, it is clear that they aim to continue the conversation
in the public eye, so we are left with no choice but to do the same."

CCSD board member Courtney Waters, one of the four who voted against Gallien's suspension, said the
superintendent was suspended because of a complaint made by an employee who doesn't report to him.

Online meetup groups for dog owners explodes in popularity

Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson, another board member who voted against the suspension, said it was a complaint
claiming a hostile work environment that was "solely and largely" about "work responsibilities in CCSD."

Before the board voted to suspend Gallien, the nine members unanimously voted to hire an outside firm to
investigate the complaint.

During the same meeting, the board also voted 5-4 to effectively dismantle the district's health advisory committee
and to not make interim chief academic officer Michelle Simmons' job permanent.

The five-member majority said in their statement that they voted to place Gallien on leave to preserve the integrity
of the district's investigation.

"Our genuine desire to do so should be evidenced by the commitment to obtaining a firm only after consultation with
Dr. Gallien's attorneys and should be further supported by our expediency in hiring the firm, which has already
occurred," they said.

With regards to the chief academic officer's post, they said their vote was based on their desire to hire someone
who possessed a degree and background in curriculum and instruction, as well as experience in a range of K-12
setting. They also wanted Gallien to give the board his recommendation after interviewing candidates.

Simmons has served as interim chief academic officer since 2022. She worked for the district for two decades,
serving as both a teacher and a principal before coming to the administration office. Her backers note that she's
also a Charleston native who attended the area's K-12 schools.

The five-member faction also said that they didn't intend overhauling the health care advisory board to be
disruptive.

"However, the bylaws state clearly that terms of membership are 'at the pleasure of the Board,' " they said. "While
we recognize this board is largely split, the slate of members was approved by a majority of the board."

Body


Former members of the Health Advisory Committee for the Charleston County School District filed a lawsuit against
the district, the school board and several individual board members for wrongful termination and violating open
meeting laws.

The lawsuit was filed Oct. 20 in response to the school board voting 5-4 to remove six members of the committee
before their terms expired during a Sept. 25 board meeting. The board voted after discussing the overhaul in
executive session, meaning the conversation wasn't open to the public.

Bonnie Cleaveland, the former committee chair and one of the plaintiffs, called the five board members who voted
to remove her the "fascist five" who were "egregiously and globally violating the law" in a statement.

Charleston Co. school board settlement talks with Superintendent Gallien up in the air

"(The Health Advisory Committee) is asking for a stay of their removals and a court-appointed babysitter for the
district to make sure they do things legally," she said.

Cleaveland and other committee members previously told The Post and Courier they believed they were removed
as retaliation for enacting a more-inclusive sexual education curriculum than the district previously had in place. A
former committee member said the old curriculum favored heterosexuality and abstinence and described anything
else as "unusual."

Cleaveland also previously noted the five board members who voted to overhaul the committee were endorsed by
the conservative parents' rights group Moms for Liberty, which has spoken out against LGBTQ education and other
issues.

The district and board didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Charleston County School District suspends Superintendent Eric Gallien, again

According to the lawsuit, the board was supposed to discuss filling five open positions on the committee during the
Sept. 25 meeting. Instead of discussing those five positions, Ed Kelley, a board member and the board's policy
liaison, proposed a slate of candidates that included six additional people.

None of the candidates' names or information were published on BoardDocs, the system the board uses to share
information, according to the suit. It alleges this violates the Freedom of Information Act, the board's policies and
procedures, and the committee's bylaws.

During the same meeting, the board voted 5-4 across the same lines to suspend Superintendent Eric Gallien and to
not make interim chief academic officer Michelle Simmons' job permanent. Gallien later sued the district for breach
of contract.

Local politicians on both sides of the aisle asked the governor and attorney general to investigate the school board
for violating open meetings laws.

The Solicitor General's Office sent the board a letter saying it had likely violated South Carolina's Freedom of
Information Act. The board held a special called meeting on Oct. 12 where members publicly debated whether to
keep Gallien on paid administrative leave before voting again 5-4 to suspend him with pay. This occurred as an
investigation is conducted into a complaint filed by a district employee accusing him of creating a hostile work
environment. Board members did not discuss the Health Advisory Committee at that meeting.

SC school report cards show academic gains. But fights on the rise.

The suit was filed by former committee members Lisa Ross, Rabbi Greg Kanter and Catherine Kaiser. It included

The committee is comprised of 13 people, including two students.

The school board members named were Kelley, board chair Pamela McKinney, Carlotte Bailey, Keith Grybowski
and Leah Whatley. Each voted to overhaul the Health Advisory Committee.

Highlight: Following a meeting that resulted in the new superintendent being placed on leave, one trustee said the

Body


Charleston County School Board member Courtney Waters had one word to describe her reaction to how the Sept.
25 board meeting unfolded: grief.

The meeting included a 5-4 vote to place Superintendent Eric Gallien - who started in his position July 1 - on
administrative leave while he is investigated for a complaint.

The meeting, like many other recent Charleston school board gatherings, left many confused and frustrated.

White also testified, via video call, telling the panel that Roberson didn't help him prepare his work proposal or make

Garvin additionally questioned whether White and Roberson could fairly be considered "associates" after he
stopped being her campaign manager once the November 2022 election ended, as Lamkin argued.

"An introduction is not a procurement decision," he repeated multiple times.

Public or private?

After an extensive exchange with the panelists over the allegations that Roberson shared emails with reporters that
were protected under attorney-client privilege, Garvin conceded that she had done so "inadvertently" at times,
without realizing the messages were privileged.

But he continued to disagree with the report's framing of other emails, which Roberson had forwarded to an email
address she said was a personal one.

Lamkin's report considered that address to be the email tied to her consulting firm, which contracted with the district
before she was elected to the board.

He described forwarding emails to that address as sharing confidential information with a vendor and providing the
firm an advantage in its work with the district. He added that his office had no way to know what happened with
emails after they were forwarded from her district account because it can't subpoena private emails.

Garvin argued that the vendor relationship the firm had with the district ended when its work with the district ended.
The email address still listed in the vendor system was just a holdover from when it was actually providing services
and being paid, he said.

It's common practice for board members to forward themselves emails in order to preserve them, Roberson
testified. She added that she didn't send the messages to anyone else.

"The evidence establishes a second email account; what the evidence doesn't establish is another vendor
recipient," Garvin said.

A mystery member

While McMaster's order charges Roberson with disclosing information from executive session, the corresponding
part of the inspector general report doesn't mention her name or that of any board member.

Instead, it cites the federal criminal indictment of former board member Kevin Hollinshead from March, which
alleges a "fellow Board of Trustees member" gave Hollinshead information from a private meeting he couldn't
participate in about the construction project for which he's alleged to have taken kickbacks.

When asked by panelists about whether Roberson was that fellow member, Lamkin said he couldn't answer, even
in a private session. He did not detail why, but said it was because of confidentiality requirements.

For Garvin, that was clear reason why she shouldn't be hit with that charge.

Section: A; news/crime; news/local state news; news; Pg. 4
Length: 595 words

Byline: Devna Bose ; , dbose@postandcourier.com
Highlight: The bulk of the Charleston County School District board's most recent meeting was spent discussing
various policy amendments.

Body


Charleston County School District board members want to pray before meetings and be given the same visitation
rights as parents to local schools.

The bulk of the board's Jan. 9 committee of the whole meeting was spent discussing various policy amendments,
including one inviting a community faith leader to open board meetings with prayer.

The amendment originally said faith leaders could not invoke "Jesus Christ" in any form or a patron saint, but board
members Carlotte Bailey and Leah Whatley said it discriminated against Christians.

Interim co-general counsel Alice Paylor recommended striking that portion.

"You don't want somebody talking about Buddha and all of that stuff," Paylor said.

Carol Tempel, a member of the school board, replied that the board needs to recognize the diversity of CCSD's
families, staff and faculty.

The amendment was changed so that faith leaders couldn't invoke any specific deity. They can only use blanket
references like God or "The Almighty," and the prayer must be nonsectarian.

The board also discussed expanding their school visitation rights. The previous policy said they could only make
official visits to schools under board authorization, but some members said they should have more ability to visit
CCSD schools since they are charged with leading the district.

The amendment makes school visits more casual, allowing members to visit any CCSD school so long as they
coordinate with the principal to find a day that works best for the school's schedule to minimize disruption.

The board reviewed another policy amendment that clarified how the general counsel should work with the board
and district, putting in writing what the general counsel can and can't do. This discussion comes after CCSD staff
attorney Mercedes Pinckney-Reese's termination in November.

Pinckney-Reese detailed concerns about new interim co-general counsels Paylor and Margaret Seymour in a Nov.
24 letter to the school board and superintendent five days before her termination. She claimed they commandeered
her staff and funneled cases to their law firm, and she specifically accused Paylor of unprofessional, bullying
behavior.
          Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR              Document 3578-13           Filed 10/16/26       Page 3 of 4
           Charleston school board may add a meeting prayer and give trustees more access to schools

The amendment says the general counsel doesn't have the authority to hire or fire CCSD employees or authorize
payments single-handedly.

The board also considered changing policy to streamline communication within the district.

They spent about an hour of the three-hour meeting discussing the amendment that would change the amount of
time it should take Superintendent Don Kennedy or members of his administration team to respond to their requests
for information.

Outside of policy amendments, the board also considered Greg Mathis Charter School's request for a district
building and discussed creating a three-person ad hoc committee to handle the superintendent search.

During committee of the whole meetings, board members vote on "initial approval" for items, which later go for "final
approval" in regular board meetings. Because the board unanimously approved expanding board members' school
access and the way the board chair is elected, those items will be on the next regular board meeting's consent
agenda and do not require further discussion.

Most committee of the whole members voted in favor of the amendments for holding prayer before meetings and
clarifying the general counsel's role, but they were not unanimously approved. These amendments will likely be
discussed again during the regular board meeting, which will be at 5:15 p.m. Jan. 23.
