Section: A; news/crime; news/local state news; news; Pg. 3
Length: 1480 words

Byline: Hillary Flynn ; , hflynn@postandcourier.com
Highlight: The Nov. 8 election increased the influence of controversial parents' rights group Moms for Liberty.

Body


Moms for Liberty, a conservative parents' rights organization, emerged as a growing political power in South
Carolina education this election cycle.

The group is known for speaking out against social-emotional learning curriculums, LGBTQ education and any
semblance of teaching critical race theory in K-12 public schools.

It made national headlines for a slew of controversies ranging from the New Hampshire chapter tweeting that they
would give a $500 reward to anyone who caught a teacher using critical race theory in their lessons, to a group of
Florida members telling MSNBC in an interview that there should be separate classes for LGBTQ and cisgender
students. They have also been associated with efforts to ban books from public school libraries, many of which
discuss LGBTQ issues and Black history.

School board candidates endorsed by the group won the majority of seats in Charleston and Berkeley counties, and
made gains in regions across the state on Nov. 8.

To an extent, this mirrors broader political trends. While the red wave heavily touted by conservative politicians
didn't sweep the country, Republican politicians were successful in many areas of South Carolina. In Charleston
County, a competitive, historically purple region, they flipped two county council seats erasing the narrowly held 5-4
Democratic majority.

Their increasing political power in South Carolina has some education community members concerned about how
their political views will impact children's education, particularly children from historically marginalized communities.

"We need to recognize that this group and some groups like them are targeting transgender people and other
members of the LGBTQ+ community, and that's very harmful," said Kristen French, a current CCSD school board
member who did not seek reelection. "In terms of that, it's so important to remember that part of a school and what
we want students to learn is how to work with others who are different from them, and be respectful and kind to
those that are different from them."

Tiffany Justice and Tina Descovich, two former school board members, started Moms for Liberty in Florida in 2021.
They both felt that parents didn't get enough voice in public schools and that their needs weren't being taken into
consideration.
           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR                 Document 3579-3              Filed 10/16/26    Page 3 of 4
                    Controversial parents' rights group Moms for Liberty increases influence in SC

This belief was exacerbated during the coronavirus pandemic when school districts nationwide switched to remote
learning, and many of those that continued teaching in-person mandated that students and staff wear masks while
in the building.

"I'm a parent, I get to direct medical care for my children," Justice said.

The organization now has 240 chapters across 42 states and over 100,000 members. There are 16 chapters across
South Carolina from Charleston in the Lowcountry, to Lexington in the Midlands and Florence in the Pee Dee and
Pickens in the Upstate.

The organization's objectives include getting parents' rights law passed in every state and eliminate critical race
theory from public school curriculums.

Critical race theory is an academic framework that examines the racism embedded in public policy and legal
institutions, and is typically taught in law schools not in grades K-12.

The group also wants to get rid of social-emotional learning, soft skills many schools are now teaching children to
help them with self-control and personal interaction. Justice believes these curriculums are a waste of school
financial resources and time. She thinks schools should be more focused on academics. Studies have shown
incorporating social-emotional learning into curriculums improves school safety and students' mental health,
something that has suffered greatly since the pandemic.

The organization also wants to push for children to read books they consider age appropriate, as well as ones they
feel aren't violating state and federal obscenity laws. Justice likened it to the age restrictions on movies and video
games.

"If it has explicit graphic sexual material, then it has no place in a school," Justice said.

When asked about the New Hampshire chapter's tweet, Justice said the wording could have been better, but if
critical race theory wasn't being taught in classrooms then it shouldn't be an issue. In regards to the MSNBC
interview with the group of Florida members, she said the women didn't believe that LGBTQ students should be
taught in separate classes, but if they were struggling with their sexuality or gender identity the teacher should
speak to them about it one-on-one or in small groups rather than discussing LGBTQ issues with the whole class.

During the election, candidates endorsed by Moms for Liberty's local chapters won five of the nine school board
seats in Charleston County and six of the eight in Berkeley. They made smaller gains in other counties, adding an
endorsed member to school boards in Beaufort, Dorchester 2, Kershaw and elsewhere.

Candidates endorsed by political parties or special interest groups are not beholden to their beliefs. In school board
races, some candidates earn nominations from multiple groups. In Charleston County, two candidates were by
endorsed by the county Republican and Democratic parties as well as the Charleston Coalition for Kids, a group
that formed in 2018 to recruit and support certain school board candidates.

Tara Wood, the chair of Charleston's Moms for Liberty, said the group first started coming together 15 months ago.
She was at a meeting in Mount Pleasant where an education expert spoke about critical race theory. After the
meeting, Wood and approximately 10 other women went up to the speaker and talked about critical race theory for
three hours. Wood said the conversation was cordial. She got the 10 women's numbers and sent out a group text
asking them if they wanted to meet for coffee sometime.

They met informally for several times discussing problems they had with education in Charleston County. Wood
agreed with Moms for Liberty's philosophies and started looking into opening a local chapter. Wood hosted the first
official Moms for Liberty meeting in August 2021.

About 60 people showed up. Now she said over 300 people sometimes attend their meetings.

Regarding local issues, the Charleston chapter is against the school district's new governance model where the
board's administrative duties will be passed to the superintendent so the board can focus more on student
academics. It is also against executive sessions, or discussion the school board can have that are not open to the
public.

Andy Pruitt, a spokesman for CCSD, said in a statement that Superintendent Don Kennedy will work with board
members to improve students' academics in the district.

"CCSD is optimistic that the development of the student outcome governance framework goals will result in
significant improvement in student outcomes and that continued efforts toward the Board-adopted goals will impact
the lives of many for years to come," he said.

The Charleston chapter's philosophy deviates slightly from its parent organization's beliefs on critical race theory.
Woods does not think that critical race theory is being taught in schools but that its tenants have trickled down into
K-12 curriculums.

"Anytime you make the narrative 'White man bad, dark man good' that's CRT and that's horrible," she said.

She is against LGBTQ education in schools and social-emotional learning curriculums, which she also believes
saps schools financial resources and class time where students could be spent learning core academics.

"What does it matter if a teacher figures out a kid is gay if he can't read?" she asked.

Keith Grybowski and Ed Kelly, two candidates Moms for Liberty endorsed who won their elections, both said that
they support parents having more voice in their children's education. They are divided over other issues, such as
the new school governance model, and are focused on students' academic performance and teacher retention.

Kelly, who was also endorsed by the Charleston County Republican Party, said that he doesn't support the new
governance model and that he is doing research into social-emotional learning.

"The job of schools is to teach reading, writing and arithmetic," he said. "If we have time to teach kids how to deal
with feelings that's terrific, but that's not our core directive."

Grybowski said that he will not second guess what the current board did in regards to the school governance model
and said that the first issue the new board will have to address is hiring a new superintendent. (Kennedy's position
was always meant to be temporary.) He added that his main goal as a board member is to improve teacher
retention.

"Without teachers, many students will not have the one-on-one literacy support they need if we are going to close
the gap," he said.

Highlight: South Carolina Governor Henry McMaster chastised members of Charleston County School Board after

Body


South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster chastised members of Charleston County School Board after a bipartisan
slew of lawmakers accused them of violating state open-meeting laws.

The board held a discussion about suspending Superintendent Eric Gallien in a closed-door executive session
during a Sept. 25 board meeting. When the board returned to the open meeting, they voted 5-4 to place Gallien on
paid administrative leave as a staff complaint against him is investigated. He has been on the job for three months.

State Rep. Joe Bustos, the Republican chairman of the Charleston legislative delegation, on Oct. 1 wrote McMaster
to ask that he have the state Office of Inspector General investigate as to whether the five members of the school
board violated South Carolina's open-meetings law after having a discussion about suspending the superintendent
in executive session.

Charleston lawmakers ask Gov. McMaster, attorney general to investigate school board

The following day, Wendell Gilliard, D-Charleston, published a letter calling on Attorney General Alan Wilson to
launch an investigation into the actions of the five school board members. He noted the faction was supported by
Moms for Liberty. The conservative parents' rights group is known for opposing LGBTQ education and critical race
theory, among other matters.

On Oct. 3, McMaster told reporters outside of the Statehouse in Columbia that conversations outside of the public
eye not only cause members of the community to lose confidence in their school boards, but also business leaders,
who may begin to second-guess their decision to move their businesses and employees into the district.

SC school districts on track to meet $3.3B relief funds deadline. But what comes next?

"The school district needs to follow the law," McMaster said. "The Freedom of Information Act is very clear.
Everybody ought to follow the law when they're asked questions that fall within the ambit of the Freedom of
Information Act; they ought to give the information out and give it out fairly quickly. It does not look to me like the
school board has done that."

Lawmakers from both sides of the aisle asked McMaster, the state inspector general and the S.C. attorney general
to investigate the board's conduct.

"If it gets worse," McMaster said about opening a state investigation. "I don't think we're at that point yet."

Bustos told The Post and Courier that he still believes an investigation is in order.

"I still believe an inquiry needs to be done, but he is the governor," Bustos said. "We must wait to see what happens
with the school board."

Gilliard called McMaster's actions "disappointing" but not surprising, and said he has never shown much care for
South Carolina's public schools, as evidence by them consistently scoring near the bottom of national rankings.

The five board members who voted to suspend Gallien - Pamela McKinney, Carlotte Bailey, Keith Grybowski, Ed
Kelley and Leah Whatley - said in an Oct. 3 statement that the board is fractured to such a degree that their
differences in opinion are being used to falsely villainize certain CCSD board members.

"We have remained largely silent in the past week, hoping our colleagues would come to conduct discussions that
promote understanding and empathy rather than exacerbate divisions," they said. "Following yesterday's press
conference and various social media posts over the last week, it is clear that they aim to continue the conversation
in the public eye, so we are left with no choice but to do the same."

CCSD board member Courtney Waters, one of the four who voted against Gallien's suspension, said the
superintendent was suspended because of a complaint made by an employee who doesn't report to him.

Online meetup groups for dog owners explodes in popularity

Darlene Dunmeyer-Roberson, another board member who voted against the suspension, said it was a complaint
claiming a hostile work environment that was "solely and largely" about "work responsibilities in CCSD."

Before the board voted to suspend Gallien, the nine members unanimously voted to hire an outside firm to
investigate the complaint.

During the same meeting, the board also voted 5-4 to effectively dismantle the district's health advisory committee
and to not make interim chief academic officer Michelle Simmons' job permanent.

The five-member majority said in their statement that they voted to place Gallien on leave to preserve the integrity
of the district's investigation.

"Our genuine desire to do so should be evidenced by the commitment to obtaining a firm only after consultation with
Dr. Gallien's attorneys and should be further supported by our expediency in hiring the firm, which has already

With regards to the chief academic officer's post, they said their vote was based on their desire to hire someone
who possessed a degree and background in curriculum and instruction, as well as experience in a range of K-12
setting. They also wanted Gallien to give the board his recommendation after interviewing candidates.

Simmons has served as interim chief academic officer since 2022. She worked for the district for two decades,
serving as both a teacher and a principal before coming to the administration office. Her backers note that she's
also a Charleston native who attended the area's K-12 schools.

The five-member faction also said that they didn't intend overhauling the health care advisory board to be
disruptive.

"However, the bylaws state clearly that terms of membership are 'at the pleasure of the Board,' " they said. "While
we recognize this board is largely split, the slate of members was approved by a majority of the board."

Body


Former members of the Health Advisory Committee for the Charleston County School District filed a lawsuit against
the district, the school board and several individual board members for wrongful termination and violating open
meeting laws.

The lawsuit was filed Oct. 20 in response to the school board voting 5-4 to remove six members of the committee
before their terms expired during a Sept. 25 board meeting. The board voted after discussing the overhaul in
executive session, meaning the conversation wasn't open to the public.

Bonnie Cleaveland, the former committee chair and one of the plaintiffs, called the five board members who voted
to remove her the "fascist five" who were "egregiously and globally violating the law" in a statement.

Charleston Co. school board settlement talks with Superintendent Gallien up in the air

"(The Health Advisory Committee) is asking for a stay of their removals and a court-appointed babysitter for the
district to make sure they do things legally," she said.

Cleaveland and other committee members previously told The Post and Courier they believed they were removed
as retaliation for enacting a more-inclusive sexual education curriculum than the district previously had in place. A
former committee member said the old curriculum favored heterosexuality and abstinence and described anything
else as "unusual."

Cleaveland also previously noted the five board members who voted to overhaul the committee were endorsed by
the conservative parents' rights group Moms for Liberty, which has spoken out against LGBTQ education and other
issues.

The district and board didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Charleston County School District suspends Superintendent Eric Gallien, again

According to the lawsuit, the board was supposed to discuss filling five open positions on the committee during the
Sept. 25 meeting. Instead of discussing those five positions, Ed Kelley, a board member and the board's policy
liaison, proposed a slate of candidates that included six additional people.

None of the candidates' names or information were published on BoardDocs, the system the board uses to share
information, according to the suit. It alleges this violates the Freedom of Information Act, the board's policies and
procedures, and the committee's bylaws.

During the same meeting, the board voted 5-4 across the same lines to suspend Superintendent Eric Gallien and to
not make interim chief academic officer Michelle Simmons' job permanent. Gallien later sued the district for breach
of contract.

Local politicians on both sides of the aisle asked the governor and attorney general to investigate the school board
for violating open meetings laws.

The Solicitor General's Office sent the board a letter saying it had likely violated South Carolina's Freedom of
Information Act. The board held a special called meeting on Oct. 12 where members publicly debated whether to
keep Gallien on paid administrative leave before voting again 5-4 to suspend him with pay. This occurred as an
investigation is conducted into a complaint filed by a district employee accusing him of creating a hostile work
environment. Board members did not discuss the Health Advisory Committee at that meeting.

SC school report cards show academic gains. But fights on the rise.

The suit was filed by former committee members Lisa Ross, Rabbi Greg Kanter and Catherine Kaiser. It included
Jim and Sue Doucher, parents of one of the student committee members.

The committee is comprised of 13 people, including two students.

The school board members named were Kelley, board chair Pamela McKinney, Carlotte Bailey, Keith Grybowski
and Leah Whatley. Each voted to overhaul the Health Advisory Committee.

Charleston County School Board member Courtney Waters had one word to describe her reaction to how the Sept.

"I never spoke to anyone about this contract," she said, noting it was "surprising" to hear years later that someone
in the district had allegedly felt pressured by her message.

White also testified, via video call, telling the panel that Roberson didn't help him prepare his work proposal or make
any money as a result of the arrangement.

Garvin additionally questioned whether White and Roberson could fairly be considered "associates" after he
stopped being her campaign manager once the November 2022 election ended, as Lamkin argued.

"An introduction is not a procurement decision," he repeated multiple times.

Public or private?

After an extensive exchange with the panelists over the allegations that Roberson shared emails with reporters that
were protected under attorney-client privilege, Garvin conceded that she had done so "inadvertently" at times,
without realizing the messages were privileged.

But he continued to disagree with the report's framing of other emails, which Roberson had forwarded to an email
address she said was a personal one.

Lamkin's report considered that address to be the email tied to her consulting firm, which contracted with the district
before she was elected to the board.

He described forwarding emails to that address as sharing confidential information with a vendor and providing the
firm an advantage in its work with the district. He added that his office had no way to know what happened with
emails after they were forwarded from her district account because it can't subpoena private emails.

Garvin argued that the vendor relationship the firm had with the district ended when its work with the district ended.
The email address still listed in the vendor system was just a holdover from when it was actually providing services
and being paid, he said.

It's common practice for board members to forward themselves emails in order to preserve them, Roberson
testified. She added that she didn't send the messages to anyone else.

"The evidence establishes a second email account; what the evidence doesn't establish is another vendor
recipient," Garvin said.

A mystery member

While McMaster's order charges Roberson with disclosing information from executive session, the corresponding
part of the inspector general report doesn't mention her name or that of any board member.

Instead, it cites the federal criminal indictment of former board member Kevin Hollinshead from March, which
alleges a "fellow Board of Trustees member" gave Hollinshead information from a private meeting he couldn't
participate in about the construction project for which he's alleged to have taken kickbacks.

When asked by panelists about whether Roberson was that fellow member, Lamkin said he couldn't answer, even
in a private session. He did not detail why, but said it was because of confidentiality requirements.

For Garvin, that was clear reason why she shouldn't be hit with that charge.

Highlight: The bulk of the Charleston County School District board's most recent meeting was spent discussing
various policy amendments.

Body


Charleston County School District board members want to pray before meetings and be given the same visitation
rights as parents to local schools.

The bulk of the board's Jan. 9 committee of the whole meeting was spent discussing various policy amendments,
including one inviting a community faith leader to open board meetings with prayer.

The amendment originally said faith leaders could not invoke "Jesus Christ" in any form or a patron saint, but board
members Carlotte Bailey and Leah Whatley said it discriminated against Christians.

Interim co-general counsel Alice Paylor recommended striking that portion.

"You don't want somebody talking about Buddha and all of that stuff," Paylor said.

Carol Tempel, a member of the school board, replied that the board needs to recognize the diversity of CCSD's
families, staff and faculty.

The amendment was changed so that faith leaders couldn't invoke any specific deity. They can only use blanket
references like God or "The Almighty," and the prayer must be nonsectarian.

The board also discussed expanding their school visitation rights. The previous policy said they could only make
official visits to schools under board authorization, but some members said they should have more ability to visit
CCSD schools since they are charged with leading the district.

The amendment makes school visits more casual, allowing members to visit any CCSD school so long as they
coordinate with the principal to find a day that works best for the school's schedule to minimize disruption.

The board reviewed another policy amendment that clarified how the general counsel should work with the board
and district, putting in writing what the general counsel can and can't do. This discussion comes after CCSD staff
attorney Mercedes Pinckney-Reese's termination in November.

Pinckney-Reese detailed concerns about new interim co-general counsels Paylor and Margaret Seymour in a Nov.
24 letter to the school board and superintendent five days before her termination. She claimed they commandeered
her staff and funneled cases to their law firm, and she specifically accused Paylor of unprofessional, bullying
behavior.
          Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR              Document 3579-13           Filed 10/16/26       Page 3 of 4
           Charleston school board may add a meeting prayer and give trustees more access to schools

The amendment says the general counsel doesn't have the authority to hire or fire CCSD employees or authorize
payments single-handedly.

The board also considered changing policy to streamline communication within the district.

They spent about an hour of the three-hour meeting discussing the amendment that would change the amount of
time it should take Superintendent Don Kennedy or members of his administration team to respond to their requests
for information.

Outside of policy amendments, the board also considered Greg Mathis Charter School's request for a district
building and discussed creating a three-person ad hoc committee to handle the superintendent search.

During committee of the whole meetings, board members vote on "initial approval" for items, which later go for "final
approval" in regular board meetings. Because the board unanimously approved expanding board members' school
access and the way the board chair is elected, those items will be on the next regular board meeting's consent
agenda and do not require further discussion.

Most committee of the whole members voted in favor of the amendments for holding prayer before meetings and
clarifying the general counsel's role, but they were not unanimously approved. These amendments will likely be
discussed again during the regular board meeting, which will be at 5:15 p.m. Jan. 23.

 2            Plaintiff Tucson Unified School District (“TUSD”) respectfully moves this Court to exclude

 3    evidence, testimony, and argument concerning nine isolated incidents of alleged misconduct by

 4    individual TUSD teachers and staff over a ten-year period. This case asks whether Defendants’

 5    platforms harmed TUSD by addicting its students. These incidents have nothing to do with that

 6    question. They are irrelevant, and any marginal value they have is substantially outweighed by the

 7    risk of unfair prejudice, confusion, and wasted time. They are inadmissible under Federal Rules of

 8    Evidence 401, 402, and 403. Tellingly, no defense expert has opined that any of these incidents,

 9    individually or collectively, caused the harms TUSD alleges.

10            Specifically, TUSD seeks to prevent Defendants from introducing any evidence of the

11    following alleged incidents:

20                with a student;

21            •   the 2017 arrest and 2018 civil lawsuit involving John Angel Corral, a security monitor,

10    spawn a series of collateral mini-trials that would confuse the issues, mislead the jury, and waste

11    the Court’s time. The Court, therefore, should exclude all of it.

12       II.      ARGUMENT

13             Evidence is admissible under Fed. R. Evid. 402 if it is relevant, meaning that the evidence

14    “has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence,” and

15    that “the fact is of consequence in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid. 401. Relevant evidence

16    may nonetheless be excluded “if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of one

17    or more of the following: unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay,

18    wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.” Fed. R. Evid. 403.

19             Under these standards, the Court should exclude all nine incidents at issue. One case

20    resulted in an acquittal, three incidents did not involve TUSD students; and all nine incidents are

21    irrelevant and excludable under Rule 403, particularly because no expert links any of them to

22    TUSD’s damages.

 3 the close of fact discovery and just a few months before trial, Tucson Unified School District

 7 designated as a document custodian, or deposed, and Defendants do not have their custodial files.

 8 The first time Tucson tried this gambit, the Court held that Tucson could not add one new witness,

 9 a student, because it waited to disclose that witness until the last day of discovery and students were

10 an entirely new category of witness not previously identified by Tucson. See June 13, 2025 CMC

11 Hr’g Tr. at 29:11–14 (“[D]oing it at the end is a problem.”). Like the proposed student witness,

12 these two new witnesses represent a new category of witnesses (school principals) that Tucson

13 heretofore has not had on its witness list, but the prejudice is even greater now than before because

14 the parties are far closer to trial and the delay is much longer.

15          The Court should strike these two new witnesses from Tucson’s witness list pursuant to

16 Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(c)(1). When the parties met and conferred on Defendants’

17 motion, Tucson claimed any prejudice can be cured because it can produce custodial files for the

18 witnesses and make them available for depositions, but that misses the point. The parties are busy

Eddie Rodriquez was arrested in October.                                                              

Since then, new details have come out about how Cholla High administrators handled the allegation
against him that was made by a then 15-year-old female Cholla student.

Rodriquez resigned when he was informed the district was working toward firing him.

He initially denied the allegations, however, school surveillance video showed him with a female
student in a stairwell.

Through the Freedom of Information Act, Tucson News Now obtained internal TUSD emails and
reports that confirm what's in police reports about the alleged incident at Cholla.

That is that it took six days for anyone to call law enforcement after the student reported she had
been assaulted.

Some of the documents contain a timeline as to what happened.

The timeline is in reports from Cholla Assistant Principal Tara Bulleigh.

According to the reports, the alleged incident happened on Monday, Oct. 17.

The next morning, Tuesday, Oct. 18, the student reported it to school administrators.

 1        I.         INTRODUCTION

 2             This trial will decide whether Defendants designed their platforms to keep students

 3    compulsively scrolling, and the damages that design caused to Tucson’s schools. It will not decide

 4    whether any schools in the Tucson Unified School District (“TUSD”) “continue[] to suffer the

 5    effects of the District’s past intentional segregation,” as a federal court found in 1977, resulting in

 6    a consent decree. Mendoza v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., 125 F.4th 1262, 1267 (9th Cir. 2025).

 7    After 50 years of litigation, that question is closed, and the court has released TUSD from the

 8    consent decree. Defendants now seek to reopen it, in a case about social media addiction, in front

 9    of the jury.

10             Defendants have made race and segregation a recurring theme of this case. In depositions,

11    Defendants have asked numerous TUSD witnesses whether racism “can” affect students, have had

12    TUSD’s superintendent narrate the history of the Desegregation Case, and have asked the District’s

13    Chief Financial Officer, a witness there to discuss the budget, why TUSD had been under a

14    desegregation order. See infra Part II.B; Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., Nos. CV-74-00090-

15    TUC-DCB, CV-74-00204-TUC-DCB (D. Ariz.) (the “Desegregation Case”). Defendants’ school-

16    administration expert now opines that “[t]he magnitude of these issues is illustrated by the

17    desegregation litigation.” 1 Ex. A. None of this concerns Defendants’ platforms. Instead, this

18    evidence presents race issues and a fifty-year-old lawsuit to the jury, inviting jurors to blame that

19    history, and therefore blame TUSD, for harms that TUSD attributes to Defendants’ platforms.

20             Four independent grounds support excluding that evidence: The Desegregation Case’s

21    findings are hearsay; Defendants’ experts cannot smuggle that information in through Rule 703, as

22    Defendants themselves asserted in Breathitt; Rule 403 favors excluding a half-century-old

23    controversy that would prejudice the jury and require a mini-trial to explain; and the Settlement

24    Agreement and the Unitary Status Plan—a plan adopted by the court to implement changes within

25    TUSD—are legal compromises that Rule 408 protects.

26    1
       All “Ex. __” references are to the Declaration of Michael Cutler in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion
27    in Limine 4, to Exclude Evidence, Testimony, and Argument Concerning Isolated Incidents of
      Alleged Racism by TUSD Staff or Students Directed at or Near TUSD Students, filed
28    concurrently.
                                                       1                              TUSD MIL NO. 3
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3583        Filed 10/16/26      Page 3 of 11




 1             TUSD does not ask the Court to pretend the court order in the Desegregation Case. TUSD

 2    asks for a narrow, two-sided ruling, like the one that already governs references to TUSD’s prior

 3    JUUL and opioid litigations. (Breathitt Cnty. Bd. of Educ. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 4:23-cv-

 4    01804, ECF No. 91; Tucson Unified Sch. Dist. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 4:24-cv-01382, ECF

 5    No. 29 at 3.) The Court should permit either side to tell the jury that a program was “required by a

 6    prior federal court order.” But the findings, agreements, and history behind that order have no place

 7    in a trial about how Defendants designed their platforms and the harms those platforms have caused

 8    TUSD.

 9       II.        BACKGROUND

10             A.     The Desegregation Case ended in 2022.

11             In 1974, two groups of families sued TUSD in the District of Arizona, alleging that its

12    schools were segregated. The court consolidated the cases in 1975, and the United States joined as

13    a plaintiff the next year. Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., 652 F.3d 1131, 1137 (9th Cir. 2011).

14    After a 1977 trial, the court found unlawful segregation at certain specific schools, and the parties

15    settled in 1978. Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., No. CV-74-00090-TUC-DCB, 2021 WL

16    1526455, at *3–4 (D. Ariz. Apr. 19, 2021). The case was inactive until the court reopened it in

17    2004. Fisher, 652 F.3d at 1137–38. In 2008, the court found that TUSD had not acted in good faith

18    under the settlement, but the court held that it would end its supervision once TUSD adopted a plan

19    for the transition. The Ninth Circuit reversed. Fisher, 652 F.3d at 1138–39, 1142–43 (holding that

20    a district must show good-faith compliance before court supervision can end). In 2013, the court

21    adopted a negotiated Unitary Status Plan (“USP”). Fisher, 2021 WL 1526455, at *5. The plan set

22    goals and requirements for TUSD in areas such as student assignment, transportation, staffing,

23    quality of education, student discipline, family and community engagement, extracurricular

24    activities, and facilities. Among other things, it led to programs and positions that remain part of

25    TUSD’s operations today, including its student relations department and restorative practice

26    facilitators. Ex. B, at 78:11–79:15.

27

28
                                                       2                                TUSD MIL NO. 3
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR             Document 3583         Filed 10/16/26     Page 4 of 11




 1              In April 2021, the court found that disparities in student discipline had been “eliminated to

 2    the extent practicable” and were not the result of past unlawful segregation or current

 3    discrimination. Fisher, 2021 WL 1526455, at *25. In July 2022, the court ended its supervision of

 4    the District. Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., No. CV-74-00090-TUC-DCB, 2022 WL 4482641,

 5    at *10 (D. Ariz. July 20, 2022). The Ninth Circuit affirmed. Mendoza, 125 F.4th at 1283. While the

 6    order was in place, TUSD paid for some of its programs through what is commonly called “910(G)”

 7    funding. Arizona law allows a school district operating under a desegregation order to budget

 8    additional funds for the costs of complying with that order. See A.R.S. § 15-910(G).

 9              B.     Defendants plan to make the Desegregation Case a trial theme.

10              Defendants’ experts plan to tell the jury that the Desegregation Case helps to explain

11    TUSD’s challenges. Dr. Michele Moore, a former superintendent, opines that the District “has long-

12    standing challenges related to racism and desegregation,” and that “[t]he magnitude of these issues

13    is illustrated by the desegregation litigation.” Ex. A, at 1. A section of her report titled “Racism and

14    Desegregation” recounts the litigation. Ex. A, at 23–25. Dr. Diana Wildermuth opines that racism

15    “obviously impacts the mental, behavioral, and social wellbeing of students in schools.” Ex. C, at

16    17. She then describes the court-ordered desegregation plan, relying on TUSD Superintendent

17    Gabriel Trujillo’s testimony about the litigation. Ex. C, at 27.

18              Defendants laid the groundwork in discovery. Their counsel had Dr. Trujillo narrate the

19    history of the Desegregation Case, Ex. D at 90:25–96:6, and had another witness read the plan’s

20    discipline provisions into the record. Ex. E, at 96:9–99:15. They even asked the District’s Chief

21    Financial Officer, a witness there to discuss the budget, why TUSD had been under a desegregation

22    order. Ex. B, at 76:12–77:9. Defendants also list “racial segregation and discrimination” among the

23    factors affecting TUSD in their summary judgment motion. (Tucson, ECF No. 16, at 1.)

24       III.        ARGUMENT

25              A. The findings in the Desegregation Case are hearsay, and no exception admits them.

26              Court orders regarding the Desegregation Case are inadmissible hearsay. A judgment from

27    another case is hearsay when offered to prove the facts it found. United States v. Sine, 493 F.3d

28
                                                          3                               TUSD MIL NO. 3
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR             Document 3583       Filed 10/16/26       Page 5 of 11




 1    1021, 1036 (9th Cir. 2007). “It is even more plain” that a judge’s specific findings are hearsay when

 2    offered for their truth. Id. The Ninth Circuit joined the Fourth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits in so

 3    holding. Id.; see also Herrick v. Garvey, 298 F.3d 1184, 1192 (10th Cir. 2002); United States v.

 4    Jones, 29 F.3d 1549, 1554 (11th Cir. 1994); Nipper v. Snipes, 7 F.3d 415, 417 (4th Cir. 1993).

 5    Courts in this Circuit apply the rule in civil cases, including on motions in limine. ICTSI Or., Inc.

 6    v. Int’l Longshore & Warehouse Union, No. 3:12-cv-1058-SI, 2019 WL 1651038, at *22–23 (D.

 7    Or. Apr. 17, 2019) (excluding prior judicial and agency decisions offered for their truth, except for

 8    facts given preclusive effect).

 9           Defendants cannot circumvent that rule. The hearsay exceptions that admit judgments cover

10    only criminal convictions and matters of personal, family, or general history or boundaries. Sine,

11    493 F.3d at 1036–37; Fed. R. Evid. 803(22), (23). The public-records exception does not reach a

12    court’s findings at all. Sine, 493 F.3d at 1037 n.16 (holding that Rule 803(8) “covers only factual

13    findings by executive branch agencies and officials, not judicial factfinding”). Nor is judicial notice

14    a backdoor: A court may notice another court’s opinion for its existence, not for the truth of its

15    findings. Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 689–90 (9th Cir. 2001).

16           Defendants want the jury to hear that a federal court found that TUSD segregated students

17    at certain schools, and then to infer that TUSD remains a place where students are treated unequally

18    because of race. That is the very use Sine forbids. Counsel also may not slip the findings in through

19    their questions. A line of “speaking” questions conveying another court’s findings “can be just as

20    improper as the direct admission” of them. Sine, 493 F.3d at 1031.

19       I.      INTRODUCTION
20            Plaintiff Charleston County School District (“CCSD” or the “District”) moves pursuant to
21    Federal Rules of Evidence 401, 402, 403, and 404 to exclude any testimony, documents, or
22    argument about (1) the history of constituent boards, including their roots in segregation; (2)
23    allegations that constituent boards made disciplinary decisions that were motivated by race or racial
24    animus; (3) allegations that constituent boards made disciplinary decisions that had a racially
25    disparate impact; or (4) allegations that constituent boards were sites of unrest or drama among
26    constituent board members.
27            The admission of such evidence would not make any material fact concerning Defendants’
28    platform design or causation of Plaintiff’s claimed damages more or less probable. Any alleged
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR            Document 3585         Filed 10/16/26     Page 2 of 10



 1    probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice, misleading the jury,

 2    and delay by inviting unnecessary “mini-trials” on collateral issues. The evidence is also

 3    impermissible character evidence. The Court should exclude this evidence under Rules 401, 402,

 4    403, and 404.

 5       II.       LEGAL STANDARD

 6              Evidence is admissible under Fed. R. Evid. 402 if it is relevant, meaning that the evidence

 7    “has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence” and

 8    “the fact is of consequence in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid. 401. Relevant evidence may

 9    nonetheless be excluded “if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of one or

10    more of the following: unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay,

11    wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.” Fed. R. Evid. 403. Finally, evidence

12    of “a person’s character or character trait” is inadmissible if offered “to prove that on a particular

13    occasion the person acted in accordance with the character or trait.” Fed. R. Evid. 404(a)(1).

14       III.      BACKGROUND

15              Prior to the landmark decision of Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, 347 U.S. 483

16    (1954), Charleston County operated multiple independent school districts, each serving a

17    geographically distinct area and distinct racial community. Act No. 340, 1967 S.C. Acts 470; see

18    also S.C. Att’y Gen. Op., Mar. 6, 2015. Like much of South Carolina, these local systems operated

19    legally segregated schools. United States v. Charleston Cty. Sch. Dist., 738 F. Supp. 1513, 1518

20    (D.S.C. 1990). After Brown, Charleston found itself in a prolonged desegregation battle. One

21    outcome of this battle was Act 340, commonly called the “Act of Consolidation,” which created a

22    single countywide district, CCSD. See id.; Act No. 340, §§ 1–7, 1967 S.C. Acts 470, 470-76.

23    However, the Act retained the prior distinct school boards as well, rebranding these as “constituent

24    districts.” Id. The Act served as a political compromise, creating more equitable countywide

25    funding and administration while retaining a significant amount of control at the local, “constituent”

26    level. See Ex. 1 to Decl. of Jessica C. Colombo in Supp. of Pl.’s Mot. in Limine #4 (“Colombo

27    Decl.”) (Charleston constituent school boards to become thing of past, Charleston City Paper (Apr.

28    17, 2025)); Colombo Decl. Ex. 4 (Valeria Nava, Gov. McMaster signs bill to abolish Charleston

                                                                    PLAINTIFF’S MOTION IN LIMINE #4 TO EXCLUDE
                                                       -2-          EVIDENCE RELATED TO CONSTITUENT BOARDS
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3585          Filed 10/16/26      Page 3 of 10



 1    County constituent school boards, Post & Courier (April 30, 2025).

 2           Needless to say, the history of segregation that initially gave rise to these local districts did

 3    not disappear overnight. According to critics, the eight constituent boards continued to serve as a

 4    vehicle for segregationist aims, whether expressly or in practice. Colombo Decl. Ex. 2 (Brian Hicks,

 5    Charleston County constituent school boards, the bell may (finally) toll for thee…, Post & Courier

 6    (Feb. 9, 2025)). The federal government ultimately intervened, filing a lawsuit alleging that the

 7    county’s mixed governance structure violated the Equal Protection Clause and helped maintain

 8    segregated schools. Charleston Cnty. Sch. Dist., 738 F. Supp. 1513 . This challenge did not succeed.

 9    In 1990, Judge Solomon Blatt rejected the principal challenge to Act 340, holding that the federal

10    government failed to prove that Act 340 was enacted with a discriminatory purpose or that the

11    alleged constitutional violations required the remedies sought. Id. at 1523. Judge Blatt’s ruling

12    largely remained in place after a trip up to the Fourth Circuit. United States v. Charleston Cnty.

13    Sch. Dist., 960 F.2d 1227 (4th Cir. 1992); United States v. Charleston Cnty. Sch. Dist., 856 F. Supp.

14    1060 (D.S.C. 1994). As a result, the constituent boards survived.

15           Constituent boards retained three primary functions: to (1) draw attendance lines; (2)

16    manage school transfers; and (3) handle student discipline appeals. Colombo Decl. Ex. 3 (Tr. of

17    May 19, 2025 Dep. of A. Huggins at 290:8-13). Over the ensuing decades, controversy over

18    constituent boards increased while their actual relevance waned significantly. Colombo Decl. Ex.

19    2 (Hicks). One investigation raised concerns that students accused of the same disciplinary offenses

20    were “met with different outcomes” depending on the constituent board in question. Emily Johnson

21    et al., Drama, accusations and unrest displayed inside Charleston Co. constituent boards, Live 5

22    News    (Feb.    8,   2025),    https://www.live5news.com/2025/02/07/drama-accusations-unrest-

23    displayed-inside-charleston-co-constituent-boards/. But another found that most disciplinary

24    decisions imposed by the constituent boards were overturned at the countywide Board level. Emily

25    Johnson, Overturned student discipline decisions in Charleston Co. schools raise concerns, Live 5

26    News (Jul. 25, 2024), https://www.live5news.com/2024/07/25/overturned-student-discipline-

27    decisions-charleston-co-schools-raise-concerns/. More generally, constituent boards became a

28    locus for “[o]ngoing drama and accusations” among constituent board members. Johnson et al.,

                                                                     PLAINTIFF’S MOTION IN LIMINE #4 TO EXCLUDE
                                                       -3-           EVIDENCE RELATED TO CONSTITUENT BOARDS
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR            Document 3585          Filed 10/16/26     Page 4 of 10



 1    supra.

 2             The foregoing ultimately led to South Carolina’s decision in 2025 to abolish constituent

 3    boards as a historical artifact and to transfer their existing powers to the countywide CCSD Board.

 4    See Patrick Phillips, Governor signs law abolishing constituent districts in Charleston County

 5    Schools, Live 5 News (Apr. 29, 2025), https://www.live5news.com/2025/04/29/governor-signs-

 6    law-abolishing-constituent-districts-charleston-county-schools/.      Constituent    boards    are    an

 7    historical oddity unique to Charleston. But they no longer exist.

 8    IV.      ARGUMENT

 9             Federal Rule of Evidence 402 precludes Defendants from introducing evidence regarding:

10    (1) the history of constituent boards, including their roots in segregation; (2) allegations that

11    constituent boards made disciplinary decisions that were motivated by race or racial animus; (3)

12    allegations that constituent boards made disciplinary decisions that had a racially disparate impact;

13    or (4) allegations that constituent boards were sites of unrest or drama among constituent board

14    members. None of that evidence has anything to do with the claims or defenses at issue in this case.

15    Even assuming it is relevant, the Court should nonetheless exclude it under Rule 403 because

16    raising evidence that necessarily draws upon Charleston’s segregationist past is unfairly prejudicial

17    and will require the time-consuming presentation of evidence with little, if any, probative value.

18    Finally, attempting to present such evidence would constitute an impermissible use of character

19    evidence and should be excluded under Rule 404.

20             A.     Historical Controversies Regarding Constituent Boards are Not Relevant

21                    Under Rules 401 and 402.

22             Evidence is only relevant if it “has any tendency” to make a fact of consequence more or

23    less probable. Fed. R. Evid. 401. Evidence concerning constituent boards does not satisfy this

24    standard.

25             Plaintiff raises a single count of negligence against Defendants. Specifically, as laid out in

26    the District’s proposed jury instructions, the District alleges that the Defendants breached their duty

27    to use ordinary care by (1) “not providing the warnings that a reasonably prudent, competent

28    company concerned with user safety would have provided”; (2) “designing, operating, and/or

      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR             Document 3585         Filed 10/16/26     Page 5 of 10



 1    marketing their social media platforms in a way that caused students to engage in problematic use,

 2    compulsive use, and/or become addicted”; (3) “deliberately targeting school-aged children, when

 3    the Defendants knew or reasonably should have foreseen the impact that doing so would have on

 4    schools”; and (4) “not designing, operating, and/or marketing their social media platforms as a

 5    reasonably prudent, safety conscious, and competent company would have done.” Dkt. 2681 at 46.

 6              There is no plausible connection between constituent boards and their history and the

 7    elements of the negligence cause of action at issue in this litigation. Nothing the constituent boards

 8    have done, and nothing about the boards’ history, has any bearing on the warnings Defendants

 9    should have provided, whether the design of their platforms caused addiction, whether they targeted

10    students, and whether they operated in a reasonably prudent manner. Any such link would be

Body


Folks have been trying to get rid of Charleston County's constituent school boards for nearly 60 years.

That is, ever since the day they were created.

But these boards, originally designed to keep local schools blissfully segregated, have been nothing if not resilient.
The Justice Department, the NAACP and a long line of state lawmakers all failed to shut them down.

Today, critics argue the eight boards are just another source of political infighting and inconsistent standards for
Charleston County students. They're not entirely wrong.

Basically, the constituent boards are collectively one big pain in the school district.

So state Rep. Joe Bustos, chairman of the county's legislative delegation, called for disbanding the boards.

"They don't do anything the district couldn't do otherwise, and they're costing us $500,000 a year," Bustos explains.
"We are the only county in the state - or the country - that has constituent school boards, and most people want to
see 'em gone."

Anyone who's followed this half-century of melodrama might expect Bustos' legislation, filed last week, to end like
all past attempts. But there are a couple of big differences now.

First, most people nowadays don't even know Charleston has constituent school boards, so there likely won't be
widespread protest. No one defended constituent boards at a recent delegation meeting, but a few showed up to
complain about them.

Second, and more importantly, Bustos has wide bipartisan support.

That all could spell doom for the constituent boards.

This matters because it could mean the district would draw attendance lines for schools - as opposed to people
elected by very few voters, under a school governance system created by the grandchildren of the people who
brought us the Civil War.

Since this is likely to become a thing, some history is in order.
           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR                 Document 3585-4            Filed 10/16/26       Page 3 of 4
               Hicks: Charleston County constituent school boards, the bell may (finally) toll for thee ...

More than a decade after the U.S. Supreme Court declared segregated schools unconstitutional, Charleston
County's various school districts were finally "consolidated." But at the same time, the old boards were transformed
into "constituent school boards."

These elected bodies were given power over personnel appointments in their schools and - most importantly - the
authority to set attendance zones.

Which meant no student could transfer from a school in one part of town to another without the blessing of two
separate constituent boards.

See how that works?

Supporters argued that, with a main school board elected countywide, constituent boards were the only way to
ensure community input. But the feds and NAACP said it was simply a ruse to keep schools segregated.

Lawsuits from the two kicked around for nearly a decade, but ultimately failed. And here we are.

A few years back, the delegation changed the Charleston County School Board to a single-member district system,
which coincidently neutered the original argument for constituent school boards.

And the school district has wrestled some control from these boards over the years. They no longer pick their own
principals and teachers, and their disciplinary rulings can be appealed to the countywide school board.

The district's position on constituent boards has been positively Swiss: It has no official position. But it's safe to say
no one at 75 Calhoun would be despondent if they were nuked ... especially since district officials told lawmakers
they could set up a single panel to hear all discipline and transfer cases.

Which would make decisions more uniform. Hint, hint.

Now, all this isn't to say there aren't some good people serving on these constituent school boards. Many of these
public servants take their jobs seriously and genuinely want what's best for Charleston County students.

Unfortunately, they're outnumbered by people with partisan agendas, outsized ambition and wildly different
standards for doing business.

You know, politicians.

Here's an example: Not too long ago, a student carried a gun into a Charleston County school. He gave it to
another student, who posed for photographs brandishing the gun on campus.

The constituent board with jurisdiction over this case decided the kid who brought the gun should be expelled, but
for whatever reason the one carrying it around was allowed to stay ... despite federal law that dictates both
should've been gone.

Yeah, the district had to step in.

Bustos is using that example pretty effectively in his arguments to colleagues. And Republicans and Democrats
mostly agree it's time to end the constituent boards, although veteran state Rep. Wendell Gilliard says they
shouldn't rush major change without weighing the consequences.

"I just want us to be fair," Gilliard says. "We need to listen to both sides."

That is a fine policy in every decision, and he's not wrong. But most of his colleagues have heard enough.

And finally, after more than half a century, the constituent school boards' luck may have run out.

   Gov. McMaster signs bill to abolish Charleston County constituent school boards
                                            Post & Courier (Charleston, SC)
                                               April 30, 2025 Wednesday

Copyright 2025 The Post and Courier All Rights Reserved

Section: A; education-lab; to-edit; Pg. 3
Length: 975 words

Byline: Valerie Nava ; , vnava@postandcourier.com
Highlight: The bill takes effect July 1. It eliminates the eight constituent boards and transfers their powers to
the centralized Charleston County School Board.

Body


Charleston County's constituent school boards, anachronisms that have persisted despite eroded oversight
powers, bureaucratic confusion and an origin story rooted in the Lowcountry's segregated past, soon will
cease to exist.

Gov. Henry McMaster signed a bill late April 28 that eliminates the county's eight constituent boards and
transfers their powers to the centralized school board. The change takes effect July 1.

The constituent boards were formed 60 years ago when schools across the county were consolidated into one
district in an effort to distribute tax revenues more equitably.

They might have been abolished then, but a compromise was struck after local residents and civic leaders
argued that they served an important purpose. As a consequence, they remained in place as advocates for
local (often rural) priorities and defenders of local interests, though their governing capabilities had been
curtailed.

In recent years, their elected members have considered student transfer requests, set attendance zones and
administered student discipline.

Over the decades, officials have debated whether to maintain the constituent boards, but no restructuring had
ensued - until now. In February, House Rep. Joe Bustos, R-Mount Pleasant, filed a bill to officially eliminate
them.

The bill soon garnered support from district administrators, several principals, teachers and parents, who
argued that internal dysfunction among board members and district staff, as well as inequities in disciplinary
actions, made management of Charleston County School District affairs unnecessarily unwieldy.

McMaster wrote in an April 28 letter to Bustos that while the state constitution prohibits legislation only
applicable to a specific county, he signed this bill into law because abolishing constituent districts in the only
county that has them will "have the same effect as any statewide bill."
          Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR                Document 3585-6             Filed 10/16/26         Page 3 of 4
                     Gov. McMaster signs bill to abolish Charleston County constituent school boards

"The General Assembly has demonstrated that it is necessary to "best meet the exigencies of (this) particular
situation." McMaster wrote. "For instance, abolishing the constituent districts will lead to more consistent
disciplinary action and result in significant financial savings."

Still, some defended the current system, arguing that the boards play a critical advocacy role that local
communities would not otherwise have.

George Tempel, constituent board member for District 3, called the loss of the boards "tragic," as vulnerable
students will lose a critical community voice to advocate on their behalf, he said. Tempel added he found it
arrogant that the legislative delegation sought to dismantle members of a public body that Charleston County
residents elected.

Future plans

Anita Huggins, Charleston County School District superintendent, said at a press conference April 29 that
district staff will work with principals to create a plan to assume the duties of the constituent boards and
present it to the district's centralized board at a committee-of-the-whole meeting on May 12.

"We are tremendously grateful for the service that these nearly 60 officials have provided," Huggins said. "We
believe they all got into this work because they wanted what was good for kids and their communities, and
we've appreciated that many of them have served in this role for decades."

The constituent boards had been proposed after the district consolidation bill got stuck in the Legislature in
1967. Many lawmakers and school officials still were avoiding, or trying to delay, desegregation. Two of the
eight original districts were predominantly White, and their members, unenthusiastic about changing the
demographics, wanted to maintain some control.

As time went on, the constituent boards were seen by many African Americans and rural residents as a
necessary vestige of an outdated bureaucratic structure because of their ability to draw attention to hyper-local
priorities and push for equitable financing. But in recent years, alleged corruption, along with the confusion
inherent in the only such decentralized legacy system in the country, turned the tide.

Rodney Lewis, a long-time constituent school board member and chair of the D-10-West Ashley board, said
the school district will need to take the proper steps to hear all student cases fairly, adding that his board
handled hundreds of discipline cases last year, on top of school transfers.

"Logistically, I want to see how a panel is going to handle all cases across the board and ensure due process,
because that's what we would have to do," he said. It's essential, he said, that students spend as little time out
of school as possible before bringing them back or placing them in one of the alternative programs.

Huggins said she believes the district is well-equipped to assume the duties associated with the constituent
boards. The district will ensure families and community members stay engaged in the process of making
student discipline and transfers a more equitable process, she said.

District officials said constituent boards' administrative costs were about $630,000 for fiscal year 2025,
including overhead costs for running meetings, salaries for district leadership liaisons and the $20 stipends
board members receive per meeting. With the dissolution of the boards, the district will save around $300,000
since it still has to account for the costs of hiring officers to join hearing panels, he said.

           Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR               Document 3585-6             Filed 10/16/26         Page 4 of 4
                     Gov. McMaster signs bill to abolish Charleston County constituent school boards

District staff members are crafting a plan, Huggins said. They might create hearing panels rather than have a
single officer handle disciplinary cases. Those panels potentially could include community members, she said.

"I'm not 100 percent sure, but this has been a part of discussions about what that will look like with principals
and internally with senior staff," Huggins said.

 1         I.         INTRODUCTION

 2              This trial will decide whether Defendants designed their platforms to keep students

 3     compulsively scrolling, and the damages that design caused to Tucson’s schools. It will not decide

 4     whether any schools in the Tucson Unified School District (“TUSD”) “continue[] to suffer the

 5     effects of the District’s past intentional segregation,” as a federal court found in 1977, resulting in

 6     a consent decree. Mendoza v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., 125 F.4th 1262, 1267 (9th Cir. 2025).

 7     After 50 years of litigation, that question is closed, and the court has released TUSD from the

 8     consent decree. Defendants now seek to reopen it, in a case about social media addiction, in front

 9     of the jury.

10              Defendants have made race and segregation a recurring theme of this case. In depositions,

11     Defendants have asked numerous TUSD witnesses whether racism “can” affect students, have had

12     TUSD’s superintendent narrate the history of the Desegregation Case, and have asked the District’s

13     Chief Financial Officer, a witness there to discuss the budget, why TUSD had been under a

14     desegregation order. See infra Part II.B; Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., Nos. CV-74-00090-

15     TUC-DCB, CV-74-00204-TUC-DCB (D. Ariz.) (the “Desegregation Case”). Defendants’ school-

16     administration expert now opines that “[t]he magnitude of these issues is illustrated by the

17     desegregation litigation.” 1 Ex. A. None of this concerns Defendants’ platforms. Instead, this

18     evidence presents race issues and a fifty-year-old lawsuit to the jury, inviting jurors to blame that

19     history, and therefore blame TUSD, for harms that TUSD attributes to Defendants’ platforms.

20              Four independent grounds support excluding that evidence: The Desegregation Case’s

21     findings are hearsay; Defendants’ experts cannot smuggle that information in through Rule 703, as

22     Defendants themselves asserted in Breathitt; Rule 403 favors excluding a half-century-old

23     controversy that would prejudice the jury and require a mini-trial to explain; and the Settlement

24     Agreement and the Unitary Status Plan—a plan adopted by the court to implement changes within

25     TUSD—are legal compromises that Rule 408 protects.

26     1
        All “Ex. __” references are to the Declaration of Michael Cutler in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion
27     in Limine 4, to Exclude Evidence, Testimony, and Argument Concerning Isolated Incidents of
       Alleged Racism by TUSD Staff or Students Directed at or Near TUSD Students, filed
28     concurrently.

 1              TUSD does not ask the Court to pretend the court order in the Desegregation Case. TUSD

 2     asks for a narrow, two-sided ruling, like the one that already governs references to TUSD’s prior

 3     JUUL and opioid litigations. (Breathitt Cnty. Bd. of Educ. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 4:23-cv-

 4     01804, ECF No. 91; Tucson Unified Sch. Dist. v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 4:24-cv-01382, ECF

 5     No. 29 at 3.) The Court should permit either side to tell the jury that a program was “required by a

 6     prior federal court order.” But the findings, agreements, and history behind that order have no place

 7     in a trial about how Defendants designed their platforms and the harms those platforms have caused

 8     TUSD.

 9        II.        BACKGROUND

10              A.     The Desegregation Case ended in 2022.

11              In 1974, two groups of families sued TUSD in the District of Arizona, alleging that its

12     schools were segregated. The court consolidated the cases in 1975, and the United States joined as

13     a plaintiff the next year. Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., 652 F.3d 1131, 1137 (9th Cir. 2011).

14     After a 1977 trial, the court found unlawful segregation at certain specific schools, and the parties

15     settled in 1978. Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., No. CV-74-00090-TUC-DCB, 2021 WL

16     1526455, at *3–4 (D. Ariz. Apr. 19, 2021). The case was inactive until the court reopened it in

17     2004. Fisher, 652 F.3d at 1137–38. In 2008, the court found that TUSD had not acted in good faith

18     under the settlement, but the court held that it would end its supervision once TUSD adopted a plan

19     for the transition. The Ninth Circuit reversed. Fisher, 652 F.3d at 1138–39, 1142–43 (holding that

20     a district must show good-faith compliance before court supervision can end). In 2013, the court

21     adopted a negotiated Unitary Status Plan (“USP”). Fisher, 2021 WL 1526455, at *5. The plan set

22     goals and requirements for TUSD in areas such as student assignment, transportation, staffing,

23     quality of education, student discipline, family and community engagement, extracurricular

24     activities, and facilities. Among other things, it led to programs and positions that remain part of

25     TUSD’s operations today, including its student relations department and restorative practice

26     facilitators. Ex. B, at 78:11–79:15.

27

28

 1               In April 2021, the court found that disparities in student discipline had been “eliminated to

 2     the extent practicable” and were not the result of past unlawful segregation or current

 3     discrimination. Fisher, 2021 WL 1526455, at *25. In July 2022, the court ended its supervision of

 4     the District. Fisher v. Tucson Unified Sch. Dist., No. CV-74-00090-TUC-DCB, 2022 WL 4482641,

 5     at *10 (D. Ariz. July 20, 2022). The Ninth Circuit affirmed. Mendoza, 125 F.4th at 1283. While the

 6     order was in place, TUSD paid for some of its programs through what is commonly called “910(G)”

 7     funding. Arizona law allows a school district operating under a desegregation order to budget

 8     additional funds for the costs of complying with that order. See A.R.S. § 15-910(G).

 9               B.     Defendants plan to make the Desegregation Case a trial theme.

10               Defendants’ experts plan to tell the jury that the Desegregation Case helps to explain

11     TUSD’s challenges. Dr. Michele Moore, a former superintendent, opines that the District “has long-

12     standing challenges related to racism and desegregation,” and that “[t]he magnitude of these issues

13     is illustrated by the desegregation litigation.” Ex. A, at 1. A section of her report titled “Racism and

14     Desegregation” recounts the litigation. Ex. A, at 23–25. Dr. Diana Wildermuth opines that racism

15     “obviously impacts the mental, behavioral, and social wellbeing of students in schools.” Ex. C, at

16     17. She then describes the court-ordered desegregation plan, relying on TUSD Superintendent

17     Gabriel Trujillo’s testimony about the litigation. Ex. C, at 27.

18               Defendants laid the groundwork in discovery. Their counsel had Dr. Trujillo narrate the

19     history of the Desegregation Case, Ex. D at 90:25–96:6, and had another witness read the plan’s

20     discipline provisions into the record. Ex. E, at 96:9–99:15. They even asked the District’s Chief

21     Financial Officer, a witness there to discuss the budget, why TUSD had been under a desegregation

22     order. Ex. B, at 76:12–77:9. Defendants also list “racial segregation and discrimination” among the

23     factors affecting TUSD in their summary judgment motion. (Tucson, ECF No. 16, at 1.)

24        III.        ARGUMENT

25               A. The findings in the Desegregation Case are hearsay, and no exception admits them.

26               Court orders regarding the Desegregation Case are inadmissible hearsay. A judgment from

27     another case is hearsay when offered to prove the facts it found. United States v. Sine, 493 F.3d

28

 1     1021, 1036 (9th Cir. 2007). “It is even more plain” that a judge’s specific findings are hearsay when

 2     offered for their truth. Id. The Ninth Circuit joined the Fourth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits in so

 3     holding. Id.; see also Herrick v. Garvey, 298 F.3d 1184, 1192 (10th Cir. 2002); United States v.

 4     Jones, 29 F.3d 1549, 1554 (11th Cir. 1994); Nipper v. Snipes, 7 F.3d 415, 417 (4th Cir. 1993).

 5     Courts in this Circuit apply the rule in civil cases, including on motions in limine. ICTSI Or., Inc.

 6     v. Int’l Longshore & Warehouse Union, No. 3:12-cv-1058-SI, 2019 WL 1651038, at *22–23 (D.

 7     Or. Apr. 17, 2019) (excluding prior judicial and agency decisions offered for their truth, except for

 8     facts given preclusive effect).

 9            Defendants cannot circumvent that rule. The hearsay exceptions that admit judgments cover

10     only criminal convictions and matters of personal, family, or general history or boundaries. Sine,

11     493 F.3d at 1036–37; Fed. R. Evid. 803(22), (23). The public-records exception does not reach a

12     court’s findings at all. Sine, 493 F.3d at 1037 n.16 (holding that Rule 803(8) “covers only factual

13     findings by executive branch agencies and officials, not judicial factfinding”). Nor is judicial notice

14     a backdoor: A court may notice another court’s opinion for its existence, not for the truth of its

15     findings. Lee v. City of Los Angeles, 250 F.3d 668, 689–90 (9th Cir. 2001).

16            Defendants want the jury to hear that a federal court found that TUSD segregated students

17     at certain schools, and then to infer that TUSD remains a place where students are treated unequally

18     because of race. That is the very use Sine forbids. Counsel also may not slip the findings in through
