 1

 2    I.     INTRODUCTION

 3           Plaintiff Tucson Unified School District (“TUSD”) moves to exclude evidence, testimony,

 4    and argument that Defendants may offer to portray themselves, their executives, or their employees

 5    as good, generous, or virtuous. That evidence falls into four categories: (1) Defendants’ charitable

 6    giving and community or school outreach; (2) praise, awards, and endorsements of Defendants by

 7    third parties; (3) stories and statistics about individuals Defendants helped, rescued, or saved, and

 8    about arrests or prosecutions attributed to Defendants; and (4) the personal philanthropy, character,

 9    and virtue of Defendants’ executives and employees.

10           Defendants offer each category for the same purpose: to persuade the jury that good

11    companies, and companies that employ good people, do not do bad things. The Federal Rules of

12    Evidence forbid that inference. Rule 404(a) bars evidence of “a person’s character or character

13    trait” offered “to prove that on a particular occasion the person acted in accordance with the

14    character or trait.” Fed. R. Evid. 404(a)(1). The evidence is also irrelevant to TUSD’s negligence

15    and public nuisance claims, which turn on how Defendants designed, operated, and marketed their

16    platforms to minors. First Am. Master Compl. ¶¶ 969–972, 1015–1018, Dkt. No. 729; Fed. R. Evid.

17    401, 402. And it is unfairly prejudicial: character evidence “subtly permits the trier of fact to reward

18    the good man and to punish the bad man because of their respective characters despite what the

19    evidence in the case shows actually happened.” Fed. R. Evid. 404 advisory committee’s note to

20    1972 proposed rules (internal quotation marks omitted); see Fed. R. Evid. 403.

21           This motion leaves Defendants free to present evidence and argument about how they

22    design and operate their platforms. 1 It seeks to bar only evidence Defendants offer for a different

23    purpose: to show that they, or the people who work for them, are good. TUSD identifies each

24    category specifically below, including by reference to evidence Meta offered in recent jury trials.

25    In one of those trials, the Tennessee court granted the State’s motion directed at this evidence and

26
      1
        TUSD does not concede the admissibility of any particular design or safety evidence, including
27    evidence of platform or policy changes made after the relevant period or adopted under agreements
      with state attorneys general, and reserves its objections to that evidence. See Dkt. No. 3239 at 2
28    (“In general, evidence regarding policy and technology changes which post-date the remedial
      period at issue will not be allowed.”).
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR          Document 3589          Filed 10/16/26    Page 3 of 10



 1    barred it from jury selection and opening statements. (Ex. A to Brane Decl., Agreed Order on

 2    Parties’ Mots. in Limine & Mots. to Strike, State ex rel. Skrmetti v. Meta Platforms, Inc., No. 23-

 3    1364-IV (Tenn. Ch. Ct. July 7, 2026), at 10.)

 4    II.    ARGUMENT

 5           A.       Defendants’ Charitable Giving and Community or School Outreach

 6           The Court should exclude evidence and argument about Defendants’ charitable giving and

 7    community or school outreach, including donations, grants, sponsorships, in-kind contributions,

 8    free resources, curricula, lesson plans, events, and awareness campaigns, offered to show that

 9    Defendants are generous or good. This motion does not bar evidence of Defendants’ outreach to,

10    and communications with, schools, parents, educators, and school-based organizations offered for

11    a non-character purpose – for example, what Defendants told or failed to tell them about the risks

12    of their platforms, or how Defendants used that outreach to market to and target minors. That

13    evidence goes to warnings, notice, marketing, and knowledge, not character. See Fed. R. Evid.

14    404(b)(2). The Court has already treated such evidence as probative of Defendants’ knowledge and

15    their targeting of school-age users. See Dkt. No. 2728 at 27:24–28:4 (outreach to “organizations

16    embedded in schools, such as the national PTA and Scholastic,” among evidence creating “triable

17    issues regarding defendants’ knowledge”); id. at 3:6–11. And if TUSD offers evidence of a specific

18    program, Defendants may respond about that program, but not with evidence of unrelated

19    philanthropy.

20           Before a jury trial this summer, Meta told the Tennessee court that it intended to offer

21    evidence of its partnerships with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children

22    (“NCMEC”), the International Bullying Prevention Association, and the Boys and Girls Club of

23    America; its campaigns with eating-disorder organizations; and technology it had given other

24    companies for free to identify harmful content. (Ex. B to Brane Decl., Meta’s Opp’n to State’s Mot.

25    to Strike Defenses & Exclude Evid., Skrmetti (Tenn. Ch. Ct. May 15, 2026), at 32–33.) At trial,

26    Meta told jurors in opening statement that it “wrote school online safety lesson plans that it gives

27    away to teachers” and “built a school partnership program to work directly with schools.” (Ex. C

28    to Brane Decl., Tenn. Trial Tr. (July 27, 2026) at 783:12–784:10.) Meta made the same free-

                                                      -3-                                    TUSD MIL NO. 5
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3589         Filed 10/16/26     Page 4 of 10



 1    technology point to the jury in a New Mexico trial. (Ex. D to Brane Decl., State ex rel. Torrez v.

 2    Meta Platforms, Inc., No. D-101-CV-2023-02838 (N.M. Dist. Ct.), Trial Tr. (Feb. 9, 2026) at

 3    1159:7–18.)

 4           Other Defendants have similar programs. Google, for example, has announced that its

 5    philanthropic arm funded “Be Internet Awesome” online-safety classroom kits for 10,000 schools

 6    nationwide. (Ex. E to Brane Decl., Google, Google.org and Highlights for Children Have Helped

 7    1 Million Students Navigate the Digital World (Apr. 1, 2026).)

 8           Defendants offer this evidence to show that they are generous—the very inference Rule

 9    404(a) forbids—and it says nothing about how they designed their platforms. Courts routinely

10    exclude it. In this District, the court in Shenwick v. Twitter, Inc. excluded evidence of “charitable

11    contributions, philanthropy, or non-profit work by or on behalf of Twitter, the Individual

12    Defendants, or any witness,” holding that “[e]vidence of good acts is irrelevant to the question of

13    whether the Twitter Defendants violated the securities laws or to the credibility of any witness.”

14    2021 WL 1232451, at *6 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 31, 2021); see also In re Nat’l Prescription Opiate Litig.,

15    2021 WL 4341317, at *2 (N.D. Ohio Sept. 23, 2021) (excluding pharmacy defendants’ in-store

16    charitable promotions and other corporate conduct unrelated to opioids as “good deeds” evidence);

17    In re Tylenol (Acetaminophen) Mktg., Sales Pracs. & Prods. Liab. Litig., 2016 WL 3125428, at

18    *11 (E.D. Pa. June 3, 2016) (holding that evidence of defendants’ “good corporate character” was

19    “not admissible in the defendants’ case-in-chief under Rule 404(a)” and that “[e]vidence of the

20    defendants’ charitable work would have no probative value”); Ruberti v. Ethicon, Inc., 2022 WL

21    17887527, at *7 (M.D. Ala. Dec. 22, 2022) (excluding manufacturer’s “community employment,

22    charitable donations, and medical contributions” over objection that the motion targeted “overly

23    broad categories of evidence rather than specific items”).

24           Outreach to schools poses a particular risk in a school district’s case, because it invites

25    jurors to see Defendants as partners to the very schools suing them. Defendants may describe such

26    programs as proof of their commitment to safety. But negligence asks whether Defendants’ conduct

27    in designing, operating, and marketing their platforms was reasonable. A lesson plan for teachers

28    does not show that Defendants reasonably designed a platform. Nor does location matter: a

                                                      -4-                                     TUSD MIL NO. 5
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3589         Filed 10/16/26    Page 5 of 10



 1    donation or education initiative in Arizona says no more about platform design than a donation

 2    anywhere else. Defendants also should not be permitted to argue that TUSD should have partnered

 3    with them instead of suing them, as Meta told the New Mexico jury: “We wish the State would

 4    partner with us rather than sue us.” (Ex. D to Brane Decl., N.M. Trial Tr. at 1189:6–11.) TUSD

 5    does not seek to exclude evidence that schools or teachers use Defendants’ platforms; that evidence

 6    bears on the platforms’ utility, not on Defendants’ character.

 7           B.      Praise, Awards, and Endorsements from Third Parties

 8           The Court should exclude evidence of praise, awards, commendations, endorsements, and

 9    letters of thanks from third parties, including government agencies and nonprofit organizations, and

10    any document or testimony describing them.

11           In Tennessee, Meta told jurors in opening statement that NCMEC’s CEO had said Meta

12    “has done more for child safety than any other tech company.” (Ex. C to Brane Decl., Tenn. Trial

13    Tr. (July 27, 2026) at 756:24–757:7.) It later elicited testimony from its executive about a

14    Department of Homeland Security letter stating that Meta’s partnership in an awareness campaign

15    “will save lives.” (Ex. C to Brane Decl., Tenn. Trial Tr. (Aug. 17, 2026) at 5398:12–5402:8.) Meta

16    invoked NCMEC’s praise again in New Mexico. (Ex. D to Brane Decl., N.M. Trial Tr. at 1178:9–

17    20.)

18           Third-party praise is character evidence delivered secondhand. Defendants offer it to show

19    that

“profits at the users’ expense,” Am. Compl. ¶ 241 — specifically, that Meta designed Instagram

to be addictive for “the benefit of Meta’s business,” id. ¶ 5, and created a misleading “impression”

that it protects teens from “harmful or inappropriate content” so it could profit, id. ¶ 357. By

Apr 01,2026 GD

Today, along with Highlights for Children, we announced that our joint initiative to fuel nationwide online safety education successfully
reached one million U.S. second-to-fifth-grade students.

With funding from Google.org, Highlights developed and deployed "Be Internet Awesome" classroom kits to 10,000 schools nationwide. The
classroom kits provide educators and families with fun and engaging educational puzzles and games designed to guide students toward safe,
healthy and positive online experiences. The initiative focuses on fundamental digital literacy, teaching kids how to be thoughtful and
responsible digital citizens, and expands our existing support of Highlights.

We believe every child should be able to learn, explore and grow safely online, and we are committed to leading the way in providing students
with the tools and training to build productive relationships with technology.

 1       I.       INTRODUCTION

 2             Plaintiff Tucson Unified School District (“TUSD”) submits this motion in limine to: (1)

 3   exclude testimony, evidence, or argument that TUSD’s reliance on external funding—or its failure

 4   to pursue other funding—reduces Defendants’ liability or TUSD’s damages, and (2) preclude

 5   testimony, evidence, or argument about how TUSD would spend a jury award. Neither topic bears

 6   on whether Defendants’ platforms harmed TUSD, or on what TUSD lost, and both would invite

 7   the jury to decide the case on improper grounds.

 8       II.      ARGUMENT

 9             A. The Court Should Exclude Evidence and Argument About TUSD’s Actual and

10                Potential Funding Sources.

11             TUSD anticipates that Defendants will argue that TUSD has sustained no financial losses

12   because the funding it relied on came from external sources. The Court should exclude this evidence

13   and argument: It would waste time, confuse the issues, and mislead the jury, and the danger of

14   unfair prejudice substantially outweighs whatever minimal probative value it has. See Fed. R. Evid.

15   403.

16             The Court should bar Defendants from arguing that TUSD cannot recover losses it paid for

17   with external funds. TUSD claims two relevant categories of damages: (1) lost time and financial

18   resources that TUSD expended responding to harms Defendants’ platforms caused (“Category 1”),

19   and (2) the cost of external programs and services that mitigate those harms (“Category 2”). (Ex.

20   A to Cutler Decl., Plaintiff’s Amended Answers to Defs.’ Third Set of Interrogatories, at 3–4) For

21   Category 1, TUSD identified the cost of teachers and staff who provide mental health and student

22   support services. (Id. at 4.) For Category 2, TUSD identified past expenditures to mitigate harms

23   from Defendants’ platforms. (Id.)

24             TUSD has funded its mental and behavioral health support and programming from a variety

25   of sources, including federal grants, state mental health funding, recoveries in other litigation, and

26   TUSD’s 910(G) desegregation levy. For instance, federal ESSER funds 1 supported social workers,

28   provided additional funding to school districts during the COVID-19 pandemic. (Ex. B to Cutler
     Decl., Trujillo Dep. at 253:1–12.)

 1   counselors, MTSS staff, 2 and TUSD’s social-emotional learning (“SEL”) curriculum. (Ex. B to

 2   Cutler Decl., 5/8/25 Trujillo Dep. at 264:1–265:6). Federal funding has supported Talkspace, a

 3   virtual mental health platform, and federal Title IV funds also helped fund the SEL department.

 4   (Ex. C to Cutler Decl., Hernandez Dep. at 51:2–56:15.) State agencies, state mental health funding,

 5   and federal grants have paid for outside mental health services for students. (Ex. D to Cutler Decl.,

 6   Carrier Dep. at 138:8–141:24.) TUSD has relied on 910(G) desegregation funding to support its

 7   student relations department. See A.R.S. § 15-910(G); (Ex. E to Cutler Decl., Warmbrand Dep. at

 8   17:7-18.) TUSD has also used recoveries from the JUUL litigation to fund related services,

 9   including behavioral health services. (Ex. D to Cutler Decl., 5/7/25 Carrier Dep. at 141:13–24.)

10          The Court should exclude all of this funding-source evidence. TUSD’s funding sources for

11   combating the harms Defendants’ platforms have caused to TUSD are irrelevant to liability.

12   Evidence is relevant only if it “has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would

13   be without the evidence” and “the fact is of consequence in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid.

14   401. TUSD claims that Defendants designed their social media platforms to addict minor users and

15   interfered with the right to public education by disrupting the classroom environment. How TUSD

16   paid to mitigate those harms says nothing about whether Defendants caused them. In other words,

17   the salary source of a counselor who spends time addressing problems Defendants’ platforms

18   caused in TUSD’s schools is irrelevant. Defendants may argue that other factors—such as the

19   COVID-19 pandemic—caused or contributed to TUSD’s injuries. This motion does not seek to

20   prevent Defendants from doing so. Instead, it seeks to bar funding sources as a proxy for alternate

21   causation. Defendants’ experts’ opinions on this point are flimsy. For instance, Dr. Moore opines

22   that because certain ESSER-funded line items overlap with expenses sought by TUSD in this

23   litigation, those expended stemmed from the COVID-19 pandemic, not social media. (Dkt. 3587-

24   3, Moore Rpt. at ¶ 86.) However, as Superintendent Gabriel Trujillo explained, ESSER funds could

 1          Having considered Plaintiff’s motion in limine No. 2, the record, and the applicable law, the

 2   Court hereby GRANTS Plaintiff’s motion in limine as follows:

 3          IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that Plaintiff’s motion in limine No. 2, to exclude references to

 4   TUSD’S sources of funding and how TUSD would spend a jury award, is GRANTED.

 5          Defendants are precluded from offering evidence, testimony, or argument (1) that TUSD’s reliance

 6   on external funding, or its failure to pursue other funding, reduces Defendants’ liability or TUSD’s

 7   damages; and (2) about how TUSD would spend a jury award.

 8          Evidence and argument about the sources TUSD used to fund its staff, services, and programming

 9   is not relevant. How TUSD paid to respond to the alleged harms does not bear on whether Defendants

10   caused them. Nor does TUSD’s use of external funds negate its claimed losses, because staff time and

11   resources devoted to responding to the alleged harms were diverted from TUSD’s educational mission

12   regardless of the funding source. Evidence of funding TUSD did not pursue would require a mini-trial

13   over grant requirements and applications, wasting time and confusing the issues. Likewise, evidence or

14   argument about how TUSD would spend a jury award has no bearing on the measure of compensatory

15   damages and risks, thereby inviting the jury to speculate. To whatever extent any of this evidence has

16   probative value, that value is substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice, confusion of the

17   issues, misleading the jury, and undue delay. Fed. R. Evid. 401, 402, 403.

18          IT IS SO ORDERED.

 1       I.       INTRODUCTION

 2             Plaintiff moves pursuant to Federal Rules of Evidence 401, 402, and 403 to exclude any

 3    testimony or documents concerning allegations of specific instances of racial discrimination,

 4    hostility, or racist conduct involving students or personnel within Tucson Unified School District

 5    (“TUSD”). These collateral events concern highly prejudicial incidents that are disconnected from

 6    TUSD’s theory of harm and Defendants’ alternative causation theories or affirmative defenses.

 7             Plaintiff seeks to exclude evidence or argument concerning the following incidents and

 8    underlying events:

 9       •     the alleged use of racial slurs by an opposing basketball team’s players and fans in 2022;

10       •     the use of racial slur directed at TUSD staff member in 2022;

11       •     the forming of Turning Points USA club at Sabino High School in 2022;

12       •     allegations of racial discrimination in the hiring of a new Borman Elementary School

13             principal in 2022;

14       •     allegations of racial discrimination in discipline of a TUSD school bus monitor in 2022;

15       •     the use of racist and derogatory language in group chat involving Sabino High School

16             students in 2020;

17       •     the allegation of a teacher using a racial slur on staff training videoconference in 2020;

18       •     the allegation of a teacher using racial slur in class in 2019.

19             The admission of evidence related to these incidents would not make any material fact

20    concerning Defendants’ platform design or the cause of TUSD’s damages more or less probable.

21    Any alleged probative value is substantially outweighed by danger of unfair prejudice, would

22    mislead the jury, and would lead to unnecessary “mini-trials” on collateral issues. This Court,

23    therefore, should exclude this evidence under Rules 401, 402, and 403.

24       II.      ARGUMENT

25             Evidence is admissible under Fed. R. Evid. 402 if it is relevant, meaning that the evidence

26    “has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence” and

27    “the fact is of consequence in determining the action.” Fed. R. Evid. 401. Relevant evidence may

28    nonetheless be excluded “if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of one or


                                                          1                            TUSD’s MIL No. 4
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR          Document 3591         Filed 10/16/26     Page 3 of 10



 1    more of the following: unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay,

 2    wasting time, or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence.” Fed. R. Evid. 403.

 3           Several of these incidents are irrelevant because they have no connection to TUSD students.

 4    In 2022, allegations were made that TUSD discriminated against an African American woman by

 5    not promoting her to principal at Borman Elementary. (Ex. A. 1) Instead, after interviewing multiple

 6    candidates, TUSD promoted an assistant principal from a TUSD middle school, who had been in

 7    that position for five years and with TUSD for several more years. Also in 2022, allegations were

 8    made that TUSD discriminated against an African American school bus monitor when it moved to

 9    terminate her employment. (Id.) The decision followed an incident where the bus driver and the

10    monitor, after completing their drop off at school, did not realize a student was still on the bus.

11    They stopped at a convenience store and left the student unattended before returning to the bus,

12    realizing the student was there, and taking the student to school. In 2020, TUSD disciplined a high

13    school principal for using the “n-word” during a staff training videoconference. (Ex. B.) The

14    training addressed the appropriate way to respond to racially inflammatory language on campus

15    and the principal used the “n-word” after warning attendees that it would be used.

16           The remaining incidents involve only a small group of students or some subset of students

17    at one school. In 2022, an opposing high school basketball team’s players and fans allegedly

18    directed racial slurs at one or more TUSD players. (Ex. C.) In response, one TUSD player posted a

19    video on TikTok of another TUSD player responding to the harassment by using a racial slur. (Id.)

20    In September 2022, a TUSD student shouted a racial slur at a TUSD staff member. There were five

21    student witnesses. (Ex. D.) The victim staff member then told another staff member that similar

22    incidents had happened before. (Id.) In August 2021, TUSD received two community complaints

23    regarding the formation of a Turning Points USA student club at Sabino High School. (Ex. E.) The

24    first complaint conveyed that “a student was experiencing emotional trauma” as a result, and the

25    second “did not speak to student experience at Sabino [High School] but did express a concern

26    regarding … property values in the community.” (Id.) In November 2020, TUSD staff received a

27
      1
       All “Ex. __” references are to the Declaration of Austin Brane in Support of Plaintiff’s Motion in
28    Limine 4 to Exclude Evidence, Testimony, and Argument Concerning Isolated Incidents of Alleged
      Racism by TUSD Staff or Students Directed at or Near TUSD Students, filed concurrently.

                                                       2                            TUSD’s MIL No. 4
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3591        Filed 10/16/26      Page 4 of 10



 1    complaint about a group chat involving Sabino High School students and students from outside

 2    TUSD. (Ex. F.) The complainant asserted, during an election cycle, that the chat contained political

 3    views that they viewed as “racist, xenophobic, homophobic, and sexist.” (Id.) In August 2019, an

 4    anonymous parent complained to TUSD about a TUSD teacher allegedly using the “N-word” in

 5    class. (Ex. G.) It is not clear how many students were present or heard the slur.

 6           A. The Incidents are Not Relevant Under Rules 401 and 402.

 7           Evidence is only relevant if it “has any tendency” to make a fact of consequence more or

 8    less probable. Fed. R. Evid. 401. These incidents do not satisfy this standard.

 9           To start, certain incidents do not involve TUSD students: the 2022 employment

10    discrimination allegations concerning an elementary school principal and a school bus monitor, and

11    the use of a racial slur by a TUSD staff member during training with other TUSD staff. Such

12    allegations do not concern the mental health of students; by definition, they are focused on the

13    employment relationship between staff and the district. As such, there is no credible argument that

14    these incidents affected the mental health or behavioral issues facing TUSD students, or that they

15    increased the disruption to the academic environment of TUSD’s schools. Any other relevance

16    Defendants may claim would be even more tenuous. Because these incidents do not relate to

17    TUSD’s students, they necessarily do not relate to whether those students compulsively used

18    Defendants’ social media platforms or suffered harm therefrom.

19           Next, allegations regarding specific instances of racial discrimination or racist conduct are

20    immaterial to any element of a claim or defense. These incidents, therefore, should be excluded

21    under Fed. R. Evid. 401, 402, and 403.

22           TUSD raises a single count of negligence against Defendants. Specifically, Plaintiff alleges

23    that the Defendants breached their duty to use ordinary care by (1) “not providing the warnings that

24    a reasonably prudent, safe, and competent company would have provided”; (2) “designing,

25    operating, and/or marketing their social media platforms in a way that caused minors to experience

26    problematic use, compulsive use, and/or addiction”; (3) “deliberately targeting school-aged

27    children, knowing of the impact that doing so could have on schools”; or (4) “not designing,

28


                                                       3                                TUSD’s MIL No. 4
      Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR           Document 3591         Filed 10/16/26       Page 5 of 10



 1    operating, and/or marketing their social media platforms as a reasonably prudent, safe, and

 2    competent company would have done.” (ECF No. 2688 at 46. 2)

 3           None of these incidents bear on whether Defendants used reasonable care. Neither a student

 4    directing a racial slur at a staff member; nor a teacher using a racial slur in front of some subset of

 5    her class; nor students at one high school forming a Turning Points USA club have any bearing on

 6    the warnings Defendants should have provided, whether Defendants designed their platforms to be

 7    addictive, or whether they operated those platforms in a reasonably prudent manner. This type of

 8    evidence “thus has no probative value.” Brown v. City of Los Angeles, 2014 WL 13130752, at *13

 9    (C.D. Cal. Oct. 27, 2014) (excluding evidence about corruption from trial about racial

10    discrimination).

11           There is also no connection between these incidents and causation—i.e., whether

12    “Defendants’ failure or failures to use ordinary care were a substantial factor in causing [TUSD] to

13    suffer harm or harms.” (ECF No. 2688 at 46). Defendants have a theory of alternative causation

14    that relates, in general terms, to race. This motion does not seek to preclude defense experts from

15    raising population-level racial disparities or discrimination in Tucson as an alternative cause of

16    TUSD’s injuries (however implausible that theory might be). But evidence—including expert

                Sabino High School.

        Findings:

            •   Students and teachers have experienced aculture and climate where racist remarks, jokes, and

            •   Counseling services are fragmented and do not address social-emotional needs.
            •   Social class divisions: students received varied support based onenrollment in AP, Honor, and
                regular classes.
            •   Some students gave concrete examples of positive teacher relationships.
            •   Some students see classroom management as an issue: describing behavior as disrespectful,
                disruptive (mask issue), offensive, and no rules or expectations.
            •   Inconsistent enforcement of rules: dress code, behavior, and classroom management.

        Recommendations:

            •   Prioritization and implementationresearch-basedCulture and Climate program focused on

            •   Normalizing culture of respect and rapport, that values the diversity of individuals race, gender,

            •   Create and engage multiple opportunities for diverse student engagement activities (e.g.

                expectations, and support principles of diversity and inclusion.

Date of Hearing: September 29, 2026

Defendants’ Motion in limine to Exclude Evidence, Argument, or
Reference to the NCOSE “Dirty Dozen” (MIL No. 2)

Tentative Ruling: The Motion is granted.


        Defendants move to exclude all evidence concerning any version of the
“Dirty Dozen” list published by the National Center on Sexual Exploitation
(NCOSE). Defendants argue that the evidence should be excluded because
it is: (1) inadmissible hearsay (and contains multiple additional levels of
hearsay); (2) irrelevant; and (3) unduly and unfairly prejudicial. Defendants
provide the following context:

        NCOSE is an advocacy group that publishes a yearly so-
        called “Dirty Dozen” list, which the group describes as a
        “campaign that calls out twelve mainstream entities” for
        allegedly “facilitating” sexual exploitation and abuse.
        Through this campaign, NCOSE targets a range of entities
        for what it considers “problematic policies and practices.”
        For example, on March 31, 2026, NCOSE named Snapchat
        and Meta’s founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg to its 2026
        “Dirty Dozen” list, as well as, among others: Chromebook,
        Android, the Apple App Store, Amazon, and Grok.

(Defs’ Mot., at p. 1, internal footnotes omitted.)



                                         1
    Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR     Document 3593-3     Filed 10/16/26   Page 3 of 4




       The “Dirty Dozen” list is obviously hearsay – an out of court statement
offered to prove the truth of its content. Plaintiffs argue that the “Dirty
Dozen” list is admissible for the non-hearsay purpose of “show[ing]
Defendants’ notice of harms resulting from their platforms, including that
platform features facilitated adult-minor contact and grooming.” (Pls’ Opp.,
at pp. 4-5.) However, when evidence of an out of court hearsay statement
is offered for a non-hearsay purpose, “the statement must be capable of
serving its nonhearsay purpose regardless of whether the jury believes the
matters asserted to be true.” (Hart v. Keenan Properties, Inc. (2020) 9
Cal.5th 442, 447, internal quotation marks and citation omitted.) The
purported relevance of the document for purposes of showing notice is
premised on the truth of the matters stated in the document, and therefore
the list is not admissible for the asserted non-hearsay purpose.

       Moreover, Plaintiffs have not shown that, under Section 230, they can
hold Defendants’ liable for facilitating adult-minor contact and grooming; the
fact that Defendants may have had “notice” that their platforms “facilitated
adult-minor contact and grooming” is thus irrelevant to the question of
whether Defendants are liable in this litigation.

       In order to attempt to avoid a hearsay exclusion, Plaintiffs claim to
offer the “Dirty Dozen” list to rebut evidence introduced by Defendants
suggesting “that child safety is a priority or that their platforms have
become safer.” (Pls’ Opp., at p. 3.) Plaintiffs make clear that this proposed
rebuttal evidence would be offered to show that Meta’s “practices have
gotten worse, not better, when it comes to protecting teens.” (Pls’ Opp., at
p. 4.) In other words, if the “Dirty Dozen” list evidence is presented to rebut
Defendants’ claim of best practices, it would be evidence “that is offered to
prove the truth of the matter stated” and thus inadmissible hearsay. (Evid.
Code, § 1200, subd. (a).)

      Plaintiffs’ other “open the door” argument fails. Plaintiffs argue as
follows:

        … if Defendants’ causation experts intend to attribute
        Plaintiffs’ mental health injuries to unwanted touching or
        other inappropriate sexual conduct in Plaintiffs’ lives,
        Plaintiffs must be permitted to cross-examine them on
        whether they considered the unwanted and inappropriate
        contact Plaintiffs experienced through Defendants’ own
        platforms as a contributing cause of those same injuries.
        Defendants cannot offer expert testimony blaming one
        source of unwanted sexual contact for Plaintiffs’ harm while
        precluding any inquiry into whether a materially similar

                                       2
    Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR      Document 3593-3    Filed 10/16/26    Page 4 of 4




        source, facilitated by Defendants’ own design choices,
        contributed to that same harm.

(Pls’ Opp., at p. 3.) Again, however, if Plaintiffs sought to introduce the
“Dirty Dozen” list to show that Defendants improperly facilitated third-party
sexual harm of Plaintiffs, Plaintiffs would be improperly relying on the “truth
of the matter asserted” in the “Dirty Dozen” list, in violation of California’s
restrictions on hearsay evidence.

       The evidence also involves a substantial risk of undue prejudice and
jury confusion. Plaintiffs have failed to identify any facts suggesting that, in
light of Section 230, Plaintiffs can hold Defendants liable for sexual harms
caused by third party users of Defendants’ platforms. The “Dirty Dozen” list
would mislead the jury into believing that Defendants’ alleged failures to
prevent sexual harms by third parties is relevant to Plaintiffs’ claims here.
Moreover, a conclusion by a third party that Defendants are responsible for
sexual harms suffered by nonparties is likely to prejudice the jurors against
Defendants and require Defendants to waste time responding to the
allegations in the “Dirty Dozen” list.

       Within the last decade, cyberbullying has emerged as a pernicious new fonn of bullying that breaks the
       spirits of our nation's children. It has been deemed a public health issue 3 and is a matter of serious concern
       to our organization.

       As you are certainly aware, cyberbullying may involve sending harassing messages (via text or Internet),
       posting disparaging comments on social networking sites, posting humiliating pictures, and other
       behaviors. 4 A meta-analysis of 80 studies examining bullying rates reported a mean prevalence rate of
       cyberbullying of 15% among 12-18 year olds.5 Recent studies have shown that cyberbullying may have
       greater adverse impacts on youth development, most likely because of the greater power imbalance created
       by the fact that victims of cyberbullying often do not (and may not ever) know their bully' s identity.6

       We are especially concerned by evidence which shows that some cyberbullying activity involves sexual
       harassment and coercion. It is our view that much of the activity referred to under the guise of"sexting"

       associated with sending and being asked for a naked image, as well as receiving a naked image without

       adults soliciting sexual images from minors, as well as criminal or abusive behavior by minors such as

Thorn’s latest research sought to understand kids’ online social networks
to better disentangle high value versus high risk relationships. In a survey
of 1,200 youth (aged 9-17), we explored young people’s attitudes and
experiences with friendships and flirting online, and how they respond to
threats of manipulation, grooming, and abuse. Four key findings emerged:



   1. Online relationships can be quite personal and meaningful — and
   for 1 in 3 young people, their closest friendships formed online.



   2. Flirting and dating online are viewed as common, even when it
   involves an adult or someone much older. While it was more common
   among teens, still roughly 1 in 3 9-12-year-olds believed it was
   common to flirt with other minors online and 1 in 5 believed it was
   common to date a young adult online.



   3. Minors are regularly encouraged to leave open forums for 1-to-1
   environments by online-only contacts. In fact, two-thirds of minors
   reported they have been asked by someone they met online to move
   from a public forum to a private conversation on a different platform.



   4. Being made to feel uncomfortable by an online connection does
   not guarantee a minor will be ready to cut off contact. Nearly one-
   quarter of kids stayed in contact with someone online who made
   them uncomfortable, with LGBTQ+ youth more than twice as likely to
   be in this position.

    REPORT PAGE

    Trends in Financial Sextortion: An
    investigation of sextortion reports in
    NCMEC CyberTipline data
    In partnership with the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC),
    this research examines more than 15 million reports made to the CyberTipline
    from 2020 to 2023 to pinpoint cases of sextortion and examine the evolving scale
    and nature of financially motivated sextortion. Importantly, while sextortion can
    affect all ages, this report focuses explicitly on the sextortion of minors.
    June 24, 2024                20 Minute Read
    SHARE




            KEY FINDINGS

                1. Sextortion, and particularly financial sextortion, continues to be a major and ongoing threat, with an
                   average of 812 reports of sextortion per week to NCMEC in the last year of data analyzed, and with reason
                   to expect that the vast majority of those reports are financial sextortion.
                2. Perpetrators leverage tactics to intentionally fan a victim’s worry about the life-changing impacts of their
                   nudes being shared—often repeating claims that it will “ruin their life.”
                3. While we find that Instagram and Snapchat are the most common platforms used for sextortion, we
                   observe trends regarding the emergence of additional end-to-end encrypted messaging apps to move
                   victims to secondary platforms and the prevalence of Cash App and gift cards for methods of payment.
                4. The two countries from which sextortion perpetrators are often operating, Nigeria and Cote d’Ivoire, make
                   use of slightly different tactics and platforms.
                5. Reports submitted by Instagram constitute a clear majority of all reports of apparent sextortion submitted
                   to NCMEC. However, there are reasons to worry whether other platforms are underreporting.

    The Rise of Financial
    Sextortion
    Between 3.5 and 5% of people are believed to have experienced
    sextortion before reaching adulthood, with girls historically more
    likely than boys to be impacted. Previous surveys have found
    demands most often were sexual or relational, including but not
    limited to demands for additional intimate imagery, engaging in
    sexual acts, or returning or staying in a romantic relationship.
    Sextortion tied to financial demands was limited, reported in less
    than 10% of cases.
    The overall trend in NCMEC reports shows a large wave of
    sextortion cases since the beginning of 2022; of the 144 million
    reports made to NCMEC that year, the hotline received 80,524
    reports of online enticement (the reporting category inclusive of
    sextortion cases), reflecting an 82% increase over the year prior.
    Although the numbers do not, on their face, differentiate among
    types of sextortion, analysis of report details demonstrates this
    increase is driven mainly by reports involving financial sextortion.

Declaration of Brian Lambert

L. My name is Brian Lambert and I make this declaration based on my personal
knowledge.
2. I received a Bachelor of Arts in Elementary Educations in 1997 from University of

Arizona and a Master of Education, Educational Leadership in 1999 from Northern Anzona

University.
3, I have 28 years experience working in K-12 education.
4, I have been Regional Assistant Superintendent at Tucson Unified School District

(“TUSD”) since July 2018 and have worked within TUSD since 1995. Before being a Regional
Assistant Superintendent, I was K-8 principal, Coordinator of Student Discipline in Student
Equity, Middle School Assistant Principal, Elementary Principal, Teacher at both Elementary and
Middle School, and a Monitor/Teacher Assistant in TUSD.

5, In my position as Regional Assistant Superintendent, I provide oversight and
collaborate with principals to address the impact of social media on school environments. This
includes responding to disruptions at the school or classroom level, supporting investigations
related to behavioral concerns, and ensuring timely and effectrve communication with parents.

6. Currently, addressing the effects of social media on TUSD is one of the biggest
challenges we address as a district. Social media permeates and exacerbates many, if not most, of
the substantial issues that students in my region’s schools are dealing with. Accordingly, a
substantial amount of my work time, and the work time of my colleagues and the school site
administrators, e.g., principals and assistant principals, that I oversee, and their staff, is spent

addressing the fallout of social media’s negative impact on students.

 Case 4:22-md-03047-YGR Document 3595-4 Filed 10/16/26 Page 3of8

7. In my experience, I have seen a growing problem of addictive, compulsive, and
problematic social media use among our students. We face a constant battle in separating students
from their phones as students are unable to regulate or control their use of social media. Both
parents and students report sleep deprivation amongst students in our school district due to
excessive social media use.

  1                                            INTRODUCTION

  2          Defendants already moved to preclude Tucson Unified School District (“Tucson”) from

  3 relying on two school principals it disclosed for the first time on its preliminary trial witness list on

  4 September 14, 2026. Now, one month after the preliminary witness lists were due and one week

  5 after Charleston County School District (“Charleston”) took the position that witnesses disclosed

  6 for the first time on the September preliminary lists were late and improper, Charleston announced

  7 that it would follow Tucson’s approach and identified Gerilyn Leland, an eighth-grade social studies

  8 teacher, as a newly disclosed trial witness. But two wrongs do not make a right.

  9          Charleston’s disclosure is improper for every reason Tucson’s is, and then some. Ms. Leland

 10 was never identified in any Plaintiff Fact Sheet, Charleston’s Rule 26 disclosures, or its interrogatory

 11 responses, and was never deposed. She was never identified as a potential document custodian, let

 12 alone selected as a document custodian for purposes of document discovery. Even worse, she was

 13 never placed on a litigation hold. And Charleston has not identified her to replace a witness who

 14 was already disclosed but is no longer available. Instead, she belongs to a category of witnesses—

 15 classroom teachers—that Charleston and the other school district bellwethers fought for years to

 16 keep off limits in discovery. Charleston’s only stated justification for identifying her (more than a

 17 month after it served its preliminary trial witness list) is that Tucson and Meta listed previously

 18 unidentified individuals on their preliminary trial witness lists. That is no justification at all. As to

 19 Meta, it withdrew its newly disclosed witnesses when Charleston challenged them, whereas Tucson

 20 has refused to withdraw its late-disclosed witnesses. Charleston cannot use one plaintiff’s actions

 21 as license for its own even more untimely disclosure. The Court should preclude Charleston from

 22 relying on Ms. Leland—or any other late-disclosed school district witness—at trial.

 23                                            BACKGROUND

 24          The parties are preparing Charleston for trial, and Charleston will proceed to trial on

 25 February 8, 2027, if Tucson’s case is resolved before then. Pursuant to the pretrial schedule, the

 26 parties filed preliminary trial witness lists on September 14, 2026. Charleston’s preliminary witness

 27 list identified five of its own employees. See Pl. Charleston Cnty. Sch. Dist.’s Prelim. Trial Witness

 28 List, ECF No. 3491 at 2–3. It did not include any teachers. The only school-level employees on

Counsel,

On yesterday’s meet and confer with Tucson, it became clear that Tucson intends to bring to trial
witnesses who were neither disclosed on their Rule 26 disclosures nor previously the subject of
discovery. It also became clear that Meta tacitly endorsed this, insofar as Meta itself had identified four
trial witnesses who were also “late disclosed.” While I am in receipt of Chris’s email from a couple hours
ago, it does not change the fundamental fact that parties on both sides seem to think there is sufficient
time to add a modest number of trial witnesses to their lists.

So, with that in mind, Charleston will take the same approach. We are hereby identifying Gerilyn Leland
as a trial witness. She is an eighth grade social studies teacher at Cario Middle School. She is expected
to testify about the impact of Defendants’ platforms on her classroom and the students she
teaches. Given that Charleston’s trial may happen as late as June, we think there is ample time for you
to receive Ms. Leland’s custodial file and take her deposition, should you wish to do so, and we will be in
touch with logistics regarding the same.

If the Defendants would like to meet and confer about this, we are of course happy to do so. We believe
any motion in limine seeking to exclude this witness should be filed tomorrow, given that the arguments
around timeliness will presumably be repeats of what you will be filing in the Tucson case. With that said,
if you would like a modest extension of time for such a motion, we would likely consent to the same.

Thanks,

                  RE:    In re: Social Media Adolescent Addiction/Personal Injury Products
                         Liability Litigation; MDL No. 3047
 Dear Counsel:

         I write on behalf of the counsel for government entity plaintiffs and the Co-Lead counsel in
 the MDL, in response to the Defendants’ 1 preservation demands to the government entity plaintiffs
 (“Preservation Demands”). Defendants’ Preservation Demands include improper demands for
 Plaintiffs to preserve documents and tangible things with little—if any—relevance to the claims
 and defenses in this action from almost every school district employee going back more than a
 decade. Complying with the Defendants’ Preservation Demand would impose an enormous
 financial and logistical burden on the Plaintiffs that far exceeds the needs of the case.

          As Defendants are no doubt aware, a party’s preservation obligations do not require the
 preservation of every shred of potentially relevant evidence or for a party to make extraordinary
 efforts to retain such evidence. Instead, courts are advised to apply the “principles of reasonableness
 and proportionality that guide discovery generally.” 2

           Defendants’ Preservation Demands go far beyond reason and any sense of proportion.

         Scope. Defendants unreasonably demand that Plaintiffs preserve “all documents,
 information (including ESI), and tangible things” on an expansive range of topics untethered to the
 issues in this case. By way of example, Defendants demand Plaintiffs preserve “disciplinary actions
 related to students for any reason.” 3 This categorical demand is unlimited by its terms. Similarly

                               Executive Summary of Opinions

1. Based on the results of the survey I conducted, it is my opinion, to a reasonable degree of
   professional certainty, that from 2014 through the present, middle school and high school
   teachers in Plaintiff’s school district have had an increasing amount of their scheduled
   classroom instruction time diverted due to the use of Defendants’ social media platforms by
   their students.

2. Results show that about a decade ago (i.e., 2014), middle school teachers in Plaintiff’s
   district spent an average of 5.5% of their scheduled classroom instruction time dealing with
   social media issues, and high school teachers in Plaintiff’s district spent an average of 4.1%
   of their scheduled classroom instruction time on these issues. This increased to 6.4% and
   8.8%, respectively, at the beginning of 2020. Once in-person teaching resumed, following
   the pause on in-person teaching due to the pandemic, the diverted time was 12.9% for
   middle school teachers and 14.9% for high school teachers. Last school year (i.e., 2023-
   2024), middle and high school teachers spent an average of 9.2% and 13.7%, respectively,
   of their scheduled classroom instruction time on this issue. Middle school teachers report
   that currently 7.1% of their classroom instruction time is diverted and high school teachers
   report 4.3%. Later in this report, I will present the detailed results for surveyed middle and
   high school teachers at various times from 2014 to the present.

14. I was asked by counsel for Plaintiff to design, execute, and analyze a market research
    survey to measure the time middle school and high school teachers employed by Plaintiff
    have been forced to divert from teaching due to student use of social media.

                                         Survey Methodology

15. The survey was designed and conducted according to generally accepted principles of
    survey research, as set forth in the Federal Judicial Center’s Manual for Complex Litigation1
    and Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence.2 These include:

        •   whether the population was properly chosen and defined;
        •   whether the sample chosen was representative of that population;
        •   whether the data gathered were accurately reported;
        •   whether the data were analyzed in accordance with accepted statistical principles;
        •   whether the questions asked were clear and not leading;
        •   whether the survey was conducted by qualified persons following proper interview
            procedures; and
        •   whether the process was conducted so as to ensure objectivity (e.g., that
            respondents were unaware of the sponsor of the survey and how the results would
            be used).
16. Additionally, to ensure objectivity in survey responses, it is standard practice to conduct
    surveys in a “double-blind” manner (i.e., withhold information about the purpose and
    sponsor of the survey from both the interviewer and the respondent).3 The survey I designed
    for this assignment satisfied this condition. The main questionnaire did not provide any
    information about the actual purpose of the survey. In addition, the screening questions in
    the survey included response options unrelated to the survey’s purpose to disguise the
    “correct” answer for qualification. Furthermore, the survey was conducted via a programmed
    internet questionnaire, eliminating the need for a human interviewer. Internet-based surveys
    remove any “interviewer bias” that may result from the way a human interviewer may
    inadvertently bias a respondent’s answer by their phrasing of the question or their reaction
    to the answer provided.

17. To ensure the meaningfulness of survey responses, it is standard survey practice to instruct
    respondents not to guess. The survey I designed satisfied this condition as well, in that the
    instructions at the beginning of the survey stated, “Thank you for your willingness to

       Pursuant to Local Civil Rule 56.1, Defendants OpenAI and Microsoft respectfully submit this Response to Plaintiffs’

Corrected Statement of Undisputed Material Facts in Support of their Motion for Partial Summary Judgment. ECF No. 1985

(News) (the “Statement”).

       Plaintiffs’ Statement fails to comply with Local Civil Rule 56.1(a). That rule requires that a motion for summary

judgment “be accompanied by a separate, short, and concise statement, in numbered paragraphs, of the material

facts as to which the moving party contends there is no genuine issue to be tried.” Local Civ. R. 56.1(a) (emphasis added).

That is not what Plaintiffs did. Plaintiffs submitted 940 [1,825] separately numbered paragraphs spanning nearly 160 [440]

pages. Such a voluminous submission does not comply with the local rule. Tripathy v. McCloskey, No. 21-CV-6584 (CS),

2024 WL 2135623, at *1 (S.D.N.Y. May 13, 2024) (striking plaintiff’s 356-page submission for “ignor[ing] the Rule’s

requirement that a statement be short and concise”). Plaintiffs’ approach has made it extremely difficult for Defendants to

respond fully while also providing their responses in a format useful to the Court.

       To deal with this massive and improper Statement, Defendants have attempted to streamline their response for the

benefit of the Court as follows:

       Undisputed/Disputed/Disputed in Part. Every fact includes one of these responses, to make clear Defendants’

position under Local Rule 56.1(b). Facts designated “Undisputed” are facts that Defendants have elected not to dispute solely

for purposes of Plaintiffs’ Motion for Summary Judgment in this matter, but does not constitute a binding admission for

any other purpose. Facts designated “Disputed” or “Disputed in Part” are facts that Defendants are disputing.

       In addition, Defendants have included certain objections and other responses to Plaintiffs’ facts where appropriate.

Those additional responses and the authority supporting those responses are identified below. For the Court’s convenience

and to avoid further lengthening this response, Defendants do not repeat their supporting authority for these issues in every

response. Instead, Defendants state these objections plainly for ease of review and incorporate the below authority into each

of those responses. Where warranted and helpful for the Court, Defendants also provide additional, paragraph-specific

information to assist the Court’s assessment.

       Immaterial. Facts designated “Immaterial” are facts that, even if true, do not help resolve any question currently

before the Court on summary judgment, i.e., they do not “affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law.” I.M. v.

United States, 362 F. Supp. 3d 161, 190 (S.D.N.Y. 2019). Rule 56.1 statements are “immaterial” if they “do not provide any

basis to rule in favor of either party for summary judgment even if they are disputed.” See Parks v. Lebhar-Friedman, Inc.,

No. 04-cv-7133-DCP-KNF, 2008 WL 3833802, at *4 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 11, 2008). Facts designated as “Immaterial” below thus

reflect facts that are not legally significant because it does not impact an element of any claim or defense at issue in Plaintiffs’

summary judgment motion. Defendants’ designation of certain facts as “immaterial” does not concede that any fact not

designated as such is material for purposes of adjudicating Plaintiffs’ Motion, or for any other purpose.

       “Not Supported by Cited Evidence.” Facts designated as “Not Supported by Cited Evidence” are facts with

incorrect citations or where the cited evidence does not support the stated fact. Holtz, 258 F.3d at 74 (A “Rule 56.1 statement

is not itself a vehicle for making factual assertions that are otherwise unsupported in the record. Where ... the record does

not support the assertions in a Local Rule 56.1 statement, those assertions should be disregarded and the record reviewed

independently.”).

       “Not Supported by Admissible Evidence.” Facts designated as “Not Supported by Admissible Evidence” are

facts that are not supported by admissible evidence as required by Local Rule 56.1, and therefore are not properly before the

Court. S.D.N.Y. Local Rule 56.1(d) (“Each statement by the movant … must be followed by citation to evidence that would

be admissible[.]”); Epstein v. Kemper Ins. Companies, 210 F. Supp. 2d 308, 314 (S.D.N.Y. 2002) (statements in a Rule 56.1

statement “are inappropriate if they are not based on personal knowledge, contain inadmissible hearsay, ... or do not cite to

supporting evidence”).
